items.title: Generative AI-Supported Learning, Cognitive Offloading, and Metacognitive Awareness: Examining Changes in Students’ Learning Regulation
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and knowledge: smart innovation orchestrators leading Chinese manufacturing firms towards innovation performance
items.abstract: Purpose Firms are highly dependent on digitalization of their processes and procedures through the integration of generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI). Gen AI supports digital innovation (DI), which is crucial to innovation performance (IP). The purpose of this study is to examine how Gen AI capabilities, the knowledge creation process (KCP), and DI contribute to the creation of IP. Furthermore, the paper discusses the moderating effects of human and AI (AI-HI) collaboration, top management knowledge value (TMKV), and big data knowledge management (BDKM). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected via questionnaires from managers of Chinese manufacturing firms. PLS-SEM is used for hypothesis testing. Findings The findings indicated that Gen AI capabilities and KCP are significantly associated with DI. Similarly, DI influences innovation performance, and DI mediates the relationships among Gen AI capabilities, KCP, and IP. Furthermore, AI-HI collaboration moderates between Gen AI capabilities and DI. Similarly, TMKV moderates between KCP and DI. Lastly, BDKM moderates between DI and innovation performance. Practical implications The study provides actionable insights for managers and policymakers on the surge in Gen AI capabilities in decision-making. Originality/value Based on resource orchestration theory (ROT), this research paper examines how the orchestration of digital and knowledge resources enhances performance.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and University Students' Critical and Higher-Order Thinking Outcomes: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review and Thematic Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot into higher education has raised urgent questions about their effects on students' higher-order cognitive abilities. While these tools promise unprecedented access to information and cognitive support, growing concerns have emerged regarding the potential erosion of critical thinking skills among university students who adopt them uncritically. Despite increasing scholarly attention to artificial intelligence in education, systematic evidence on how generative AI relates to distinct dimensions of higher-order thinking remains limited. This systematic literature review, guided by the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, aims to identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on the relationship between generative AI use and university students' analytical, evaluative, and creative thinking outcomes, using the higher-order cognitive processes of Bloom's Revised Taxonomy as an organizing framework. A comprehensive search across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar yielded 847 initial records, of which 42 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria after screening. Thematic synthesis revealed heterogeneous outcomes: analytical thinking outcomes were generally positive under structured prompting conditions, evaluative thinking appeared most vulnerable in the absence of deliberate pedagogical design, and creative thinking outcomes were most frequently reported as positive. Across themes, the quality of pedagogical integration was the condition most frequently associated with favorable outcomes. This review contributes a dimension-level synthesis of generative AI and higher-order thinking, identifies the pedagogical conditions associated with favorable and unfavorable outcomes, and documents the heterogeneity of outcomes across studies, offering an evidence-informed framework for educators, curriculum designers, and policymakers seeking to use generative AI as a cognitive scaffold rather than a cognitive replacement.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence use for academic writing in English among Kuwaiti nursing and health sciences students in a mixed methods study
items.abstract: Abstract Research on generative AI use in EMI nursing and health sciences contexts in the Gulf region remains limited. This study investigated the uses, experiences, and perceptions of generative AI among nursing and health science students at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET) in Kuwait. Using a single-institution convergent mixed methods survey design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected from 241 undergraduate students. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that 94.6% of participants reported previous use of generative AI tools and 83.4% reported using them for academic purposes at least occasionally. Four interrelated themes emerged: (1) AI as a facilitator of English academic writing; (2) AI as a cognitive and academic efficiency tool; (3) AI as a confidence-building resource; and (4) students’ awareness of opportunities and risks associated with AI use. Students primarily used AI to improve grammar, vocabulary, idea generation, and writing organization. Participants also reported greater perceived confidence and reduced writing anxiety. Furthermore, participants expressed awareness of concerns regarding overreliance, inaccurate information, and academic integrity. The study contributes to emerging research on AI in higher education by highlighting students’ reported use and perceptions of AI in EMI health science contexts in Kuwait. The findings suggest the need for AI literacy frameworks that promote responsible and ethical use of AI in academic writing.

items.title: Generative Health Data Science for Data-to-Dose Precision Pharmacology: A Critical Methodological Review and Translational Framework
items.abstract: Precision pharmacology aims to select the most appropriate medicine, dose and monitoring strategy for an individual patient.Its translation is limited by fragmented records, incomplete biological characterization, timevarying physiology and the difficulty of converting high-dimensional evidence into a safe action.Generative health data science extends conventional prediction by learning structured representations of molecules, cells, patients and clinical trajectories and by producing reviewable candidates such as molecular structures, treatment options, synthetic records, counterfactual courses and dose scenarios.This critical review evaluates large language models, multimodal and biological foundation models, graph and diffusion architectures, syntheticpatient generators, digital twins and bounded agentic workflows across target discovery, repurposing, pharmacogenomics, treatment selection, individualised dosing and pharmacovigilance.Evidence is strongest for representation learning, structure-enabled discovery and selected pharmacogenomic pathways; autonomous patient-level treatment and dosing remain investigational.Recent advances include explainable drug-repurposing foundation models, multimodal clinical foundation models and a randomised phase 2a trial of a generative-AIdiscovered TNIK inhibitor.We propose a Data-to-Dose framework linking intended-use definition, data provenance, longitudinal patient-state modelling, constrained generation, mechanistic and causal checks, uncertainty-aware ranking, professional review and lifecycle monitoring.Generation must remain distinct from clinical authorisation, and synthetic-data fidelity must not be equated with privacy, fairness or external validity.Generative systems may become an enabling layer for precision pharmacology only when their creative capacity is bounded by pharmacology, evidence and accountable clinical judgment.

items.title: Gesture-based rehabilitation as an assistive technology for post-infectious and post-critical illness disabilities: opportunities and challenges
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This commentary examines gesture-based rehabilitation (GBR) as an assistive technology within an ecosystem for survivors of infectious diseases with neurological disabilities. It describes the roles of computer vision, markerless motion capture, depth cameras, artificial intelligence-driven pose estimation, wearable sensors, smartphone-based tracking, and virtual or augmented reality, while considering infection control and global accessibility. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This commentary was developed by synthesising the existing literature, with an emphasis on camera-based motion capture, gesture-controlled serious games, AI-driven pose estimation, wearable movement sensors, smartphone tracking, and virtual or augmented reality rehabilitation systems. The analysis compares outcomes from traditional neurological conditions, such as stroke and Parkinson's disease, to the specific needs of infectious disease survivors. RESULTS: Evidence from stroke, Parkinson's disease, and other neurological populations suggests that gesture-based systems may support motor rehabilitation, patient engagement, and remote monitoring. GBR may also reduce the need for direct patient-therapist interaction. However, there is currently insufficient direct evidence on the effectiveness, safety, and feasibility of these systems among survivors of infectious diseases. Additional barriers include hardware costs, limited digital infrastructure, and unequal access in rural and resource-constrained settings. CONCLUSION: GBR offers a versatile method for aiding recovery after infectious neurological illnesses. Nonetheless, its safety, effectiveness, and practicality in these groups remain uncertain, as most evidence comes from non-infectious neurological conditions. Specific studies on these populations are necessary before routinely recommending these technologies, along with strategies to overcome technological, financial, and access-related challenges.

items.title: Global advances in Generative AI for renewable energy and implications for sustainable energy transitions in Africa
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being investigated for renewable-energy forecasting, optimisation, predictive maintenance, synthetic-data generation, and infrastructure planning. This study reviews global advances and critically assesses their implications for Africa's sustainable energy transition. It aims to: (i) map GenAI applications in renewable-energy systems; (ii) distinguish demonstrated results from proposed African opportunities; (iii) evaluate evidence quality, transferability, and deployment feasibility; and (iv) identify context-specific research and policy priorities. A systematic review was reported using PRISMA 2020, with the PRALSMA AI-assisted workflow used to support, but not replace, researcher-led screening and synthesis. OpenAlex records published from 2020 to May 2026 were screened, yielding 75 included studies. Manual analysis was triangulated with ChatGPT Project and NotebookLM, and findings were weighted by methodological quality, evidence maturity, and relevance to African data, grid, infrastructure, institutional, and cost conditions. The corpus remains geographically imbalanced: five of the 75 included studies report an African institutional affiliation (Morocco, Nigeria, and South Africa, with further co-affiliations in Tunisia and Gabon), and most quantitative outcomes still derive from non-African simulations, prototypes, or case studies. Consequently, reported error, cost, emission, and accuracy improvements are treated as source-specific rather than directly transferable African effects. Near-term priorities are controlled pilots of lightweight, explainable, offline-capable decision support and synthetic-data methods; compute-intensive diffusion, agentic, digital-twin, and imitation-learning applications require further validation. GenAI may support African renewable-energy transitions, but benefits depend on local datasets, reliable fallback procedures, lifecycle environmental assessment, workforce capacity, governance, and staged field validation.

items.title: Governing critical AI capabilities through sovereign orchestration without full stack ownership
items.abstract: Abstract AI increasingly depends on globally distributed infrastructures, including advanced semiconductors, cloud platforms, data centres, foundation models, software frameworks and specialised labour. This dependence has intensified policy interest in AI sovereignty, which is often associated with domestic ownership of technological assets and the development of a nationally controlled AI stack. This article argues that ownership is neither a sufficient nor universally necessary condition of sovereign control. Instead, AI sovereignty should be understood as the capacity of public authorities to govern the dependencies through which critical AI capabilities are produced, accessed and sustained. The article develops the concept of functional AI sovereignty and identifies six interdependent dimensions of effective sovereign control: visibility, authority, allocation, substitutability, continuity and accountability. It then introduces sovereign orchestration as an institutional model through which governments can coordinate heterogeneous public and private AI resources using regulation, strategic procurement, interoperability, multi-provider routing, capacity clearing and selective public ownership. This model seeks to preserve access to private investment, international supply chains and distributed expertise while preventing individual providers from acquiring an irreversible veto over critical public functions. The article also specifies the limits of functional sovereignty. Orchestration requires sufficient public-sector expertise, access to operational information and credible technological alternatives. Direct ownership remains necessary where interruption costs are high, substitution is infeasible and external legal or geopolitical exposure is substantial. Effective AI sovereignty therefore lies not in eliminating technological interdependence, but in ensuring that critical dependencies remain visible, reversible, resilient and publicly accountable.

items.title: Green Software Metrics and Tools: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The increasing energy consumption of the Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) sector and the growing carbon emissions demonstrate the importance of sustainable software engineering practices. This study presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) covering the years 2020 to September 2025 to review and analyze research on green software metrics, tools, and validation methods. This study addresses five research questions, focusing on (i) green metrics, (ii) their place within the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), (iii) validation methodologies, (iv) measurement tools and models, and (v) the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The results obtained reveal that energy-focused metrics are widely discussed in the literature. Instruments and empirical experiments represent the most common methodological approaches used for validation. While emerging models demonstrate the place of machine learning in predictive energy forecasting, the use of AI remains limited, and standardized frameworks are lacking.

items.title: Guia de assistência fisioterapêutica na atenção básica
items.abstract: Primary Health Care (PHC) is the main gateway to the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), being responsible for health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and care coordination. In this context, this study aimed to develop a practical physiotherapy care guide to support physiotherapists working in PHC. This is a review based on documents from the Brazilian Ministry of Health and scientific evidence, addressing the main conditions managed at the primary care level, including low back pain, pneumonia, asthma, headache, epilepsy, repetitive strain injuries/work-related musculoskeletal disorders (RSI/WMSDs), and occupational health-related dysfunctions. The guide compiles assessment strategies, evidence-based physiotherapeutic interventions, referral criteria, and clinical flowcharts designed to support clinical decision-making. The findings highlight that physiotherapists enhance the effectiveness of PHC through individual and group interventions, home visits, health education, and participation in multidisciplinary teams. It is concluded that incorporating practical protocols and care strategies strengthens comprehensive care, promotes disease prevention, and contributes to improving functionality and quality of life among individuals receiving primary health care services.

items.title: Harnessing AI for Competitive Advantage: A Novel Lean-Agile Supply chain for the Indian Technical Textiles Sector
items.abstract: The primary Indian technical textiles industry concern is to keep market responsiveness and attain operational efficiency, which will rank as a $22 billion business in 2024 ( Grand View Research, 2024 ). The study suggests the implementation of lean-agile enabled supply chain framework as part of the artificial intelligence that has been combined with hybrid lean-agile manufacturing to improve the competitive advantage of Indian technical textile-based manufacturing companies. This study conducted through theoretical synthesis of the Resource-Based View theory, Dynamic Capabilities framework, and supply chain innovation theory illustrates that a variety of AI technologies, such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and real-time optimization, enable lean efficiency targets as well as the agile responsiveness objectives to be met in parallel. The framework determines that there are four essential AI-enabled capabilities which include intelligent demand forecasting, adaptive inventory optimization, predictive quality management and dynamic supplier collaboration. According to synthesized research, organizations applying such AI-driven models demonstrate significant performance gains, including up to 87% forecasting accuracy , 93.45% defect detection rates , 65% faster disruption response times , and 24.9% reductions in aggregate inventory costs. The proposed model provides both theoretical advancement in understanding AI‘s role in supply chain strategy and practical implementation guidance for technical textile manufacturers seeking digital transformation.

items.title: Harnessing business value from artificial intelligence through dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical microfoundations
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to automate repetitive business processes, enhance employee capabilities and augment managerial decision-making across industries. However, many organisations struggle to translate AI initiatives into sustained strategic value. This gap between AI's potential and realised outcomes highlights the need to understand how organisations harness AI to generate business value, which this paper addresses. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a two-phase qualitative study of Transport and Logistics (T&L) organisations grounded in dynamic capabilities theory and its microfoundations. The first phase involved a systematic review of practitioner (grey) literature to examine AI applications, capabilities, processes and benefits across five T&L organisations. Phase 2 triangulated and refined these insights through key informant interviews. Findings The results indicate that T&L organisations adopt both generic AI technologies (e.g. chatbots, virtual assistants) and industry-specific AI-enabled systems (e.g. autonomous guided vehicles in warehouses, robotic forklifts and collaborative robots). When these AI assets are combined with specific microfoundations, such as AI skills, organisational routines and governance processes, they enable organisations to develop AI-based dynamic capabilities to sense, respond and transform transport, warehousing and delivery operations. These capabilities contribute to workers' safety, operational efficiency, customer experience and environmental sustainability. Originality/value The study contributes a model and propositions that explain how AI-based dynamic capabilities, underpinned by sociotechnical microfoundations enable organisations to gain operational and environmental advantages, offering guidance for managers embarking on an AI exploration journey.

items.title: Healthcare-related challenges of the taxi industry stakeholders in the city of Tshwane, South Africa
items.abstract: Introduction: The minibus taxi industry underpins South Africa's public transport system, serving approximately 80.2% of daily commuters. Despite its economic importance, the sector operates in a high-stress, informal environment, exposing drivers to occupational health risks compounded by limited medical surveillance. This study explored healthcare-related challenges and barriers to healthcare access among taxi drivers, owners, and association representatives in the CoT. Methods: A participatory research design was used. Ninety-two participants (83 males, 9 females) were purposively sampled from taxi drivers, owners, and association representatives across CoT taxi ranks. Data were collected using eight focus group discussions, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using framework-informed, deductive thematic analysis. Results: Findings revealed layered systemic barriers: regulatory gaps, institutional distrust, and gendered stigma; geographic and infrastructural constraints, absent mental health services, and power imbalances between owners and drivers; conflicts between clinic hours and work schedules, rejection of medical certificates, and broken referral pathways; and deferred care, self-medication, and accumulated psychological strain. Conclusion: Taxi rank environments and rigid industry structures directly threaten drivers' physical and psychological well-being, fostering fatigue, substance use, and unresolved trauma. Interventions should prioritise decentralised, mobile healthcare aligned with operational hours and improved rank infrastructure to promote safer, dignified working conditions.

items.title: Hierarchical Safe and Robust UAV Path Planning Based on Large Language Models
items.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path planning is widely applied in fields such as Internet of Things (IoT) environmental monitoring, intelligent transportation, low-altitude logistics, and autonomous inspection. With the rapid development of UAV intelligence, natural language task planning powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising research hotspot. However, in safety-critical flight missions, LLMs suffer from issues such as unstable structured outputs, insufficient understanding of complex constraints, and unreliable responses to dangerous inputs, which can jeopardize the safety and robustness of UAV path planning. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an LLM-based hierarchical safe and robust UAV path planning framework to achieve co-optimization of natural language task understanding and deterministic path search. We design a Prompt–RAG–Validator safety enhancement mechanism that improves the LLM’s safety decision-making capabilities through prompt constraints, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and rule validation, while constructing a structured constraint representation to convert natural language requirements into parsable planning constraints. Furthermore, we combine a grid cost map with the A* algorithm to achieve autonomous obstacle avoidance and safe grid-path generation. In addition, a two-stage evaluation system targeting both the constraint generation layer and the path-planning layer is constructed to verify model output reliability and actual planning performance. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method across various complex scenarios, including multi-constraint tasks, risk-zone planning, incomplete input information, and prompt injection attacks. Notably, on the current template-derived benchmark, the deterministic regex/slot parser provided a stronger baseline with no dangerous outputs, whereas the LLM-based pipeline offers greater flexibility in handling diverse linguistic expressions.

items.title: Homo tokenatus: The Human Equipped with Tokens in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: Lee Gyoo Baek, Professor Emeritus, University of Ulsan (울산대학교 디자인건축융합학부 명예교수) This paper proposes Homo tokenatus, "the human equipped with tokens," as a concept for the human condition in an era when generative AI has become the basic infrastructure of everyday life. Large language models read the world in tokens and learn and speak by predicting the next token; the token is both the mode of being of AI and the unit by which its use is measured and priced. The paper structures the concept on three levels: technology (the nature of AI), economy (the unit of use), and humanity (the mode of life). It distinguishes the concept from Homo economicus, Phono sapiens, Homo silicus, and Homo Promptus, and discusses the problems of quantification, inequality, dependence, and value raised by a society in which human thought and labor are converted into tokens. items.title: How AI Transparency Affect Manufacturing Employee Decision Quality: A Stress Cognitive Appraisal Perspective
items.abstract: Human–AI collaboration supports manufacturing sustainability by minimizing time loss and resource waste, thereby enabling faster, more accurate decision-making. However, how AI transparency influences employee decision quality through cognitive appraisal remains underexplored, limiting guidance on balancing technological advancement with employee decision-making in manufacturing. Drawing on stress cognitive appraisal theory, this study examines the relationship between AI transparency and employee decision quality using structural equation modeling of questionnaire data from 321 intelligent manufacturing employees. Results show that AI transparency enhances employee decision quality by promoting challenge appraisal and reducing threat appraisal; both appraisals mediate this relationship. AI-enabled job complexity moderates the negative effect of AI transparency on threat appraisal and significantly moderates the mediating role of threat appraisal. However, its moderating effect on the relationship between AI transparency and challenge appraisal is nonsignificant. These findings provide practical guidance for developing and implementing human-centered AI systems in manufacturing to improve employee decision quality.

items.title: How Effectively Can AI Enhance Predictive Accuracy and Smart Grid Performance in Renewable Energy Systems?
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a transformative role in enhancing predictive accuracy and operational performance in renewable energy systems. As the global shift toward sustainable energy intensifies, AI enables improved efficiency, reduced costs, and greater reliability across energy infrastructures. This study investigates AI's potential to optimize energy production forecasting, consumption patterns, and smart grid operations. Using a methodological approach that combines a comprehensive review of AI applications and real-world case studies, the research evaluates techniques such as predictive analytics, deep learning, and real-time grid optimization. Findings reveal that AI significantly enhances forecasting accuracy, system adaptability, and real-time energy management. By integrating AI, renewable energy systems become more resilient and efficient, supporting long-term sustainability goals. The study offers strategic insights into how AI technologies can be effectively leveraged to advance renewable energy development and intelligent grid performance.

items.title: How Humans and AI Detect Deepfakes Differently: Complementary Strategies for Human-AI Teaming
items.abstract: Deepfakes are AI-generated synthetic media that manipulate individuals’ lip movements, facial expressions, and voices, creating serious risks through deception, misinformation, and identity misuse. Although AI-based tools are essential for Deepfake detection, understanding and strengthening human detection ability is equally important. We compare human and AI attention allocation patterns, showing that they rely on distinct cues and reasoning strategies. We also examine physiological differences across levels of AI literacy to identify factors associated with superior human performance. Contrary to the assumption that AI consistently outperforms humans in Deepfake detection tasks, individuals with greater prior AI exposure may rival or exceed AI-based detectors in certain contexts. Eye-tracking and EEG evidence further suggests that humans use holistic, intuitive, and flexible visual-cognitive processing to detect subtle inconsistencies and artifacts overlooked by AI. These findings clarify how humans and AI process deceptive visual cues differently and inform trustworthy, adaptive human-AI teaming for Deepfake detection.

items.title: How Reliable Is AI at Applying A Priori Codebooks? A Systematic Review and Reliability-Generalization Meta-Analysis of AI–Human Agreement in Deductive Qualitative Coding
items.abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to apply deductive, theory-driven ("a priori") codebooks to qualitative data, and justify this with AI–human agreement statistics. Those statistics vary widely, depend strongly on how often each code occurs, and are rarely compared with human–human agreement on the same codes. This systematic review and meta-analysis will (1) estimate typical AI–human agreement (Cohen's κ) in a priori coding across education, health, business, and the social sciences; (2) estimate the gap between AI–human and human–human agreement within studies; (3) test whether agreement varies with field, code type, code prevalence, model, prompting strategy, and comparison target; and (4) describe how completely studies report what is needed to interpret agreement. Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 and REGEMA.

items.title: Human Control of Advanced AI Agents: A Six-Dimension Framework and Evidence Review
items.abstract: This standalone working paper proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing meaningful human control of advanced AI agents. It examines authorization, containment, intervention, oversight, propagation, and situational grounding through five illustrative pilot cases and supplementary public-source analysis. The evidence review includes unintended actions against real external systems, monitoring studies, software disclosures, governance responses, and prospective assessments, with explicit source limits. Real-world effects, controlled evaluations, and simulations are distinguished. The supplementary Philadelphia false-tip case has unresolved severity. This edition reissues project research with presentation and metadata changes; it does not report new experiments. The framework remains conceptual, unreviewed, and empirically unvalidated. items.title: Human Situational Awareness and Workload during Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicle Hazard Monitoring: A Cross-Platform Study
items.abstract: As autonomous ground and aerial vehicles become increasingly capable, human operators are transitioning from direct control to supervisory monitoring roles. Maintaining Situational Awareness (SA) during rare but safety critical hazard events remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when operators must monitor heterogeneous autonomous platforms with different spatial and cognitive demands. This study develops a unified experimental framework for investigating human SA and workload during supervisory monitoring of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under hazard conditions. Eighteen participants completed six within-subject conditions combining three interface modalities, namely, visual-only, haptic-only, and visual-haptic, with two platform types, ground vehicle and aerial drone. SA was measured using Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART), while workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The key findings are: 1) Aerial monitoring produced significantly lower overall SA, higher situational demand, and greater workload than ground monitoring, driven by elevated Demand and reduced Understanding rather than diminished Supply. 2) Workload was consistently coupled with situational demand across all conditions, suggesting a stable SA-workload mechanism. 3) Both haptic-only and visual-haptic significantly improved overall SA relative to visual-only without increasing workload, demonstrating that interface design can enhance awareness within the existing workload envelope. These findings establish a cross-platform behavioural baseline for designing multimodal interfaces that enhance operator SA without elevating workload in heterogeneous autonomous vehicle systems.

items.title: Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence in Health Professions Education and Decision-Making
items.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms health professions education and clinical decision-making through human-centered and sociotechnical systems (STSs) principles. It defines four key affordances (informational, inferential, relational, and organizational) that determine how AI affects learning, collaboration, and care. In education, AI can enhance competency-based medical education through adaptive learning, simulation, and automated assessment, expanding educators’ capacity for feedback and curriculum improvement. In clinical practice, AI can support diagnosis, risk prediction, and workflow coordination but requires transparency, validation, and ethical oversight to maintain trust and professional autonomy. Case studies such as Google Flu Trends and IBM Watson for Oncology show that most failures arise from poor implementation rather than technical limitations. Integrating human-centered design and STS frameworks, the chapter emphasizes the need for co-design, cybersecurity awareness, and accountability as central for effective innovation, ensuring AI supports and enhances human judgment and professional practice rather than replacing or undermining them.

items.title: Human–AI Task Redistribution in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redistributing academic work among humans, AI, and human–AI collaboration, raising questions about which tasks learners should continue performing independently. This mixed-methods study examined task allocation using survey data from 317 university students representing 974 recurring academic tasks and interviews with 24 faculty members across 24 disciplines. Student data showed substantial movement from human-only performance toward joint human–AI and AI-delegated work. Task redistribution was significantly associated with perceived skill demands and learning opportunities. Faculty strongly supported preserving independent practice for foundational, embodied, and high-stakes activities while permitting AI for appropriate peripheral, advanced, and efficiency-oriented tasks. Integrating both datasets produced a Human–AI Task Allocation Model organized around a Training Zone–Performance Zone principle. The findings suggest that appropriate AI delegation should depend on learners’ developmental stage, task purpose, and retained capacity for verification, judgment, and accountability.

items.title: HYENAISM: An Emergent Concept in the Political, Social, and Cultural Domains
items.abstract: HYENAISM An Emergent Concept in the Political, Social, and Cultural Domains Ali Jabar Rashidi Professor, Visiting Faculty Member, Supreme National Defense University, Iran Email: a.j.rashidi@gmail.com ORCID: 0009-0006-0371-1408 October 12, 2026 Abstract Exclusively self-interested behavior and actions that disregard humanistic and ethical boundaries are increasingly emerging and spreading among certain individuals, organizations, groups, and countries across various social, political, economic, cultural, and even scientific and technological domains, at local, national, and particularly international levels, including relations among states. Such conduct, which has historically been regarded as unacceptable within human societies, appears to be gaining a degree of normalization and legitimacy. Since these forms of convergence often cross humanistic and ethical boundaries and cannot be clearly captured within conventional classifications of human behavior and action, I propose the term “Hyenaism” to describe this phenomenon, based on my examination and study of its characteristics. Hyenaism is a proposed term for describing opportunistic convergence among actors who, under other circumstances, may be rivals, adversaries, or distrustful of one another. These actors align themselves around shared material or non-material interests and objectives, or a combination of both. To advance such convergence, they may collectively mobilize or exploit a range of capabilities and resources, institutions, laws and rules, narratives, and forms of power. The duration and life cycle of such convergence are not fixed; rather, they depend on the continuation of shared interests and on whether the expected benefits remain at an acceptable level for the participating actors. This original conceptual note presents the definition and conceptual dimensions of Hyenaism as proposed by the author, with the aim of making the concept available for use by researchers and other interested parties. Keywords: Hyenaism; Opportunism; Tactical Alliance; Collective Self-Interest; Institutional Power; Coalition Life Cycle. 1. Definition of Hyenaism Hyenaism is a political, economic, social, military, and cultural pattern of brazen opportunism and collective self-interest in which individuals, groups, countries, political parties, formal or informal organizations, and local, national, or international institutions—which may ordinarily be enemies or rivals—temporarily or conditionally converge to achieve a shared goal, pursue common interests, seize an opportunity, or capture common prey. Shared interests and objectives may be material, non-material, or a combination of both. To facilitate this convergence, participants may coordinate, employ, manipulate, or exploit available instruments and capabilities, including military, political, and economic power; consensus-building and influencing public opinion at local, national, and international levels; mass mobilization; various organizations and institutions; laws, rules, and procedures; culture; poverty, vulnerability, and dependency; science and technology; and other available resources and means. The defining characteristic is not the mere presence of any particular instrument, but rather the opportunistic and potentially exploitative coordination of efforts to secure a common benefit—even when the participants have a history of hostility toward one another or lack enduring friendship and shared values. 2. Scope and Types of Actors in Hyenaism The actors involved in Hyenaism are not limited to individuals or informal groups. They may include any of the following, or combinations thereof: · Individuals, networks, factions, and social groups; · Political parties, movements, and coalitions; · Countries, government bodies, and public officials; · Formal and informal organizations and institutions at local, national, and international levels; · Cross-sectoral coalitions comprising governmental, non-governmental, economic, cultural, scientific, or other actors. This term constitutes an analytical framework and should not be applied indiscriminately to every alliance or form of cooperation. Its application to a specific case requires evidence of opportunistic convergence, the role of shared interests, and the coordinated use of leverage and capabilities. One of its distinguishing features is insufficient adherence to humanistic and ethical considerations in the objectives, methods, and actions associated with the convergence. Hyenaism may constitute the hidden face of certain forms of convergence whose publicly visible and declared image presents purportedly humanitarian and ethical objectives, including opposition to oppression, even when such claims are fabricated or contrived. Consequently, identifying Hyenaism is a strategic undertaking that depends on sufficient situational awareness and a comprehensive intelligence picture. 3. The Nature of Shared Interests and Objectives in Hyenaism The interests and objectives that bring actors together may be material—such as wealth, territory, resources (for example, energy resources, oil, water, and the like, in the case of countries), market access, commercial objectives, or institutional superiority—or non-material, such as sovereign domination, colonization, subordination through dependency, status, legitimacy, influence, identity, and cultural or religious interests. They may also involve a combination of both. The expected benefits do not have to be exactly the same for all participants; in some cases, it is sufficient for each participant to perceive some benefit for themselves arising from the convergence and its temporary arrangements. In certain Hyenaism scenarios, a dominant actor or driving force may also induce other actors to join through the exercise of physical, political, economic, or institutional coercion, thereby paving the way for a broader convergence of multiple actors. 4. Instruments and Mechanisms for Realizing Hyenaism In a Hyenaistic convergence, participants may coordinate or exploit multiple instruments, including, but not limited to, the following: · Military, political, diplomatic, and economic power; · Consensus-building, agenda-setting, and influencing public opinion at local, national, and international levels; · Mobilization of communities and populations, social constituencies, and organized networks; · Deployment or functional capture of organizations and institutions at local, national, and international levels; · Laws, rules, procedures, regulatory systems, and their selective interpretation; · Cultural narratives, symbols, traditions, and identity frameworks; · Poverty, vulnerability, dependency, or inequalities in access to resources; · Science, technology, information, expertise, and control over knowledge; · Any other capability or resource that can be coordinated in pursuit of a shared objective. The presence of any one of these instruments does not, in itself, imply misconduct. The central question is whether such instruments are collectively and opportunistically employed or exploited to secure a shared advantage at the expense of broader principles, other parties, or the public interest. 5. The Logic of Alliances and Temporary Convergence in Hyenaism Hyenaism describes a form of instrumental alignment: when a common goal, opportunity, or interest comes to the fore, previous hostilities may be temporarily suspended. This does not necessarily imply that fundamental disagreements have been resolved. Cooperation may be tactical, selective, covert, or overt, while competition continues in other domains. 6. Life Cycle and Conditions for the Termination of Hyenaism The life cycle of Hyenaism depends primarily on two interrelated conditions: first, the continuation of shared interests or objectives among the participants; and second, the expected benefit remaining above each participant’s threshold of acceptability, as determined by its cost–benefit considerations or economic, political, or cultural viability. Such convergence may weaken or dissolve when the common opportunity disappears, costs increase, benefits are distributed unequally, risks intensify, or participants’ objectives diverge. If the underlying incentive structure changes, the convergence may transform into a different type of coalition, with a smaller or otherwise different membership than the original group. Thus, Hyenaism is not a permanent organization, but rather a conditional and potentially terminable pattern of alignment. 7. Multilevel Scope: The actors involved may be individuals, groups, political parties, countries, or institutions operating at any scale. Diversity of Objectives: Shared interests may be material, non-material, or a combination of both. Multi-Instrument Coordination: Various sources of power and influence may be deployed in a coordinated manner. Conditional Continuity: The survival of the convergence depends on shared interests and the continued acceptability of the net benefit to its participants. External Ethical and Institutional Consequences: The pursuit of shared benefits typically imposes costs on others, the public interest, established rules, or broader principles. 8. Conventional cooperation may be transparent, principled, accountable, and directed toward a legitimate public good. items.abstract: Recursive AI, the prospect of artificial intelligence taking an increasingly complete role in building and improving artificial intelligence, has so far been demonstrated mostly on small models, bounded tasks, and fixed time budgets. items.title: Identification of letters distorted by physiologically-inspired spatial scrambling
items.abstract: In the geniculostriate pathway of the human visual system, neuronal projections carry signals from a particular retinal locus in parallel from one anatomical area to the next. Imprecision in the fidelity of these projections would place constraints on the ability of the system to perform tasks requiring positional information. We investigated the impact that "spatial scrambling" between stages would have on visual performance. We consider two stages in a simple canonical model of the early visual cortex where scrambling might occur: either the input to the first orientation-tuned mechanisms (analogous to V1 simple cells), or the output from those mechanisms. These are referred as "subcortical" (SCS) and "cortical scrambling" (CS). We developed a wavelet decomposition and resynthesis algorithm to mimic these effects, and measured human performance in letter identification affected by the two types of scrambling. Our results showed SCS and CS have distinguishable effects on both perceived noisiness of letters and letter identification threshold. Comparing human performance against a suite of pre-trained and custom convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that were trained on the scrambled stimuli, relative efficiency (calculated from the ratio of human:CNN thresholds) is higher for CS than SCS. However, in modelling human inefficiency by reducing the proportion of wavelets available to the CNNs, humans are less efficient in CS than SCS. These differences in efficiencies show humans are better at processing orientation redundant stimuli (CS) than orientation noisy stimuli (SCS). We hypothesize this reflects differences in integration properties at the input and output stages of simple cells in the cortex.

items.title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
items.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

items.title: Immediate effects of dynamic- and static-based custom insoles on structural alignment, pressure distribution and subjective comfort in paediatric flexible flatfoot
items.abstract: Background Customised insoles for paediatric flexible flatfoot are typically designed using static foot postures, which may fail to reflect the dynamic mechanical demands of gait. This study explored an alternative method, evaluating whether dynamically modelled insoles, captured during active locomotion, can effectively provide optimized kinematic control and plantar load distribution while maintaining ergonomic comfort as compared to traditional static designs. Methods Two insoles were customised for 15 children (8–10 years) with flexible flatfeet: a static-based insole (SI), modelled during seated great toe dorsiflexion, and a dynamic-based insole (DI), modelled from the active arch profile during walking. Assessments included geometric characteristics (arch height and medial longitudinal arch [MLA] angle), rearfoot angle (RFA), peak plantar pressure (PPP), and subjective ergonomic comfort. Results DI exhibited a significantly greater arch height and MLA angle than SI. Kinematically, both designs reduced severe RFA misalignments, with DI demonstrating more consistent bilateral kinematic control. Kinetically, both functioned as effective total-contact devices, attenuating pressure peaks at the heel and lateral forefoot. Notably, despite the more pronounced structural contour of DI, participants reported high subjective comfort scores that were statistically equivalent to SI. Conclusion Both SI and DI effectively improved rearfoot eversion and reduced localized pressures without compromising subjective comfort. Specifically, the dynamic approach achieved greater total-contact load redistribution across the MLA.

items.title: Immersive reality training for oral and maxillofacial microvascular reconstruction in resource-limited settings
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction Microvascular free flap transfer is essential in contemporary oral and maxillofacial reconstruction. However, acquiring microvascular anastomosis skills remains challenging in low-resource settings due to a heavy dependence on high-cost instruments and expert supervision. This scoping review (ScR) mapped the existing evidence on immersive reality (IR) technologies for microvascular anastomosis training and explored their potential applications in educationally limited and low-resource environments. Main body Comprehensive literature searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus for studies published between 2010 and April 2026, following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Seven studies published between 2010 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria. Although these studies supported specific microsurgical tasks, most described proof-of-concept prototypes with limited validation. Furthermore, none evaluated a structured microvascular reconstruction curriculum. Crucially, no included study directly evaluated maxillofacial reconstructive surgeons or trainees, nor did any specifically address head and neck microvascular anastomosis curricula. Conclusion Current evidence indicates technical promise alongside significant literature gaps, as effectiveness, clinical transfer to the operating room, and cost-effectiveness remain unproven. To address training disparities, we introduce an author-proposed staged curriculum framework wherein lower-cost IR platforms provide foundational orientation, instrument handling, depth perception, suture sequencing, and ergonomic visualization before trainees’ progress to bench, biological, and supervised clinical training.

items.title: Implementation of a single-port robotic platform into your colorectal surgery practice: a SAGES colorectal committee task force review of evolving robotic technology and innovations
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Robotic and endoscopic techniques continue to revolutionize minimally invasive surgery. Single-port (SP) robotic platforms mark a new era in minimally invasive colorectal surgery, combining single-incision/site access with full robotic articulation through a single access point. This manuscript, as a part of a four-part series, outlines specific technical considerations of the SP robotic platform including details of the platform, instrumentation, docking, and operative maneuvers. METHODS: Subject matter experts from the SAGES Colorectal Committee SP Task Force performed a structured review of the currently FDA-approved SP robotic platform, assessing technical features, instrumentation, and workflow considerations for several key representative operations relevant to colorectal surgery. Three clinical areas of SP implementation included transanal robotic surgery, right colectomy, and low anterior resection (LAR). Task Force members (subject matter experts with early experience in SP robotic platforms) analyzed technical details, patient selection, and operative workflows. Representative procedural techniques were detailed with emphasis on instrumentation choice, docking strategies, and key operative steps specific to single-port colorectal surgery. RESULTS: The technical aspects of the SP platform include full robotic articulation through a single 25 mm port. A SP approach also enables triangulation and dexterity within confined spaces using three wristed instruments and a flexible 3-D camera. The current 360-degree boom rotation facilitates multi-quadrant manipulation without redocking. Current limitations may include continued reliance on bedside assistance for certain energy and stapling operative steps, although stapling capability has expanded with FDA clearance of an SP-compatible 45 mm stapler as of April 2025. Training of the entire operative team and gradual progression of case complexity is recommended as the surgeon implements this new technology into clinical practice. CONCLUSIONS: A SP robotic approach to minimally invasive colorectal surgical procedures is feasible for a range of colorectal surgery operations. In select procedures like SP TAMIS, SP right colectomy, and SP-LAR, the single-port platform appears to offer advantages related to reduced invasiveness and improved surgeon ergonomics compared to other minimally invasive approaches. Successful implementation requires structured training, careful patient selection, and adherence to evidence-based adoption principles.

items.title: Independent Convergence: MIT, AI, and the Future of Higher Education
items.abstract: This research note compares the January 2026 HEI 2030 Manifesto (Simpson, 2026) with MIT’s August 2026 report on AI in teaching, learning, and research training. It finds substantial independent convergence around a structural diagnosis: AI weakens the relationship between student output and demonstrated capability, requiring assessment redesign, observable performance, stronger human agency, and continuous institutional governance. The January manifesto goes further in specifying an integrated operating model linking assessment, task-level governance, credential signaling, and human-AI work. MIT develops community, mentoring, privacy, access, and implementation resources more fully. The comparison then raises a harder question: whether credible AI-era education is economically scalable overall.

items.title: Innovations in higher education: a methodology for the integration of artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence technologies, particularly generative AI and chatbots, into higher education necessitates a fundamental reconceptualization of the relationship between technological capabilities and pedagogical approaches. This article presents a comprehensive methodology for integrating artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies (digital pedagogy) into the higher education system, with a specific emphasis on content verification as a critical component for reliable AI implementation. The methodological foundations of this comprehensive methodology are based on research in the fields of educational data mining, predictive analytics, and recommender systems conducted between 2019 and 2025, providing a robust theoretical and empirical basis for the proposed methodological integration. This study synthesizes scientific developments in technical, psychological, and pedagogical research to address the challenge of ensuring the authenticity of educational content while simultaneously developing students’ critical thinking skills. The proposed methodology encompasses a conceptual framework for AI and digital pedagogy integration, a data storage architecture, algorithms for data collection and preprocessing, verification protocols for generated content, and pedagogical strategies for using verification as a learning tool. The practical significance of this research lies in the development of content verification tools and methodological guidelines for the use of AI in higher education institutions.

items.title: Installation Personas: A Persona-Centered Framework for AI-Driven Interactive Art Installations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is enabling interactive art installations to become increasingly adaptive and socially interactive, yet limited conceptual guidance exists for analyzing installations themselves as persona-like entities. In this study, the Installation Persona Framework is proposed, extending persona-centered analysis from users and individual AI agents to AI-driven interactive installations. The framework conceptualizes Persona Identity through two complementary dimensions—Persona Type and Persona Role—and examines their expression through Persona Behavior and Interaction and association with Artistic Function and Intended Audience Experience. Using a structured screening process, 41 AI-driven interactive installations were selected from 329 artworks presented at the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) AI Art Gallery from 2024 to 2026. Qualitative analysis identified seven recurring Persona Archetypes and eight higher-order Persona Role Families. An independent classification assessment carried out by four external coders showed statistically significant but fair intercoder agreement for Persona Archetype (Fleiss’ κ = 0.266) and Persona Role Family (κ = 0.203), indicating measurable but limited classification reproducibility and ambiguity in category boundaries. Because audience evaluation was not conducted, audience experience was limited to artist-intended or researcher-inferred interpretations based on available documentation. Overall, the framework provides a structured vocabulary for analyzing AI-driven interactive installations as integrated persona-like entities.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming journalism and creating challenges for journalism education. Guided by Diffusion of Innovations theory, this study examines AI integration in journalism education in Bangladesh. Using a qualitative multi-method design, the study analyzed 21 curricula from 17 universities and interviewed 18 journalism educators, including 12 faculty members and 6 department heads. Findings reveal limited formal AI integration despite educators’ recognition of its professional importance, reflecting a gap between individual recognition and institutional adoption shaped by infrastructure, expertise, funding, and policy constraints. The study highlights the need for context-sensitive curriculum reform, sustained faculty development, and practical AI training.

items.title: Integrating Human Resource Analytics into Business Education Curriculum: Perspectives of Senior Human Resource Managers in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated integrating human resource analytics into the postgraduate Business Education curriculum: Perspectives of senior human resource managers in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria. It became imperative due to the widening gap between traditional, theory-based business pedagogy and the data-driven workforce requirements of modern corporate organisations. The descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study sampled 120 senior HR managers from key economic sectors using purposive and convenience sampling methods. Data were gathered via “Human Resource Analytics Integration in Business Education Questionnaire (HRALBEQ)”, validated by HRM and Measurement and Evaluation experts, pilot-tested, and confirmed using the Cronbach’s alpha method, which yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.88. Data were analysed using mean scores and standard deviation for the research questions, and an independent t-test was used to test null hypotheses at .05 level of significance. The findings of the study revealed a critical, great extent demand from HR managers to include descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics (advanced data literacy) in the Business Education curriculum. Notably, both public and private sector managers shared identical views, providing educational policymakers with a clear road map to update the curriculum. Based on these findings, it was recommended that universities in Nigeria should establish modern, data-driven Business Education laboratories to train postgraduate students in descriptive HR metrics, enabling them to systematically collect, clean, and visualise fundamental workforce data using industry-standard tools like Power Business Intelligence and Excel. It was also recommended that tertiary institutions in the state should introduce predictive modeling for talent forecasting, and prescriptive analytics through corporate workplace learning projects.

items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), such as GPT, BERT, RoBERTa, and their variants, have significantly transformed the traditional natural language processing (NLP) by providing rich context-sensitive representation and offering sophisticated generative capabilities. Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning approach, primarily organizing unlabelled data, discover latent patterns, employed to perform tasks such as topic modelling, and document classification. The assimilation of these two domains has the capability to enhance representation learning and discovering structure in large, unannotated corpora. This research paper explores the possibility of enhancing clustering results with LLM&s;s embedding and utilizing clustering techniques to LLM outputs for better insights. The paper discusses advancement in methodology, comparative analyses, application context, and challenges. The discussion also highlights the emerging research directions that reveal the scope for embedding clustering techniques in the LLM learning process.

items.title: Interactive and inspectable LLM planning for human-in-the-loop EV battery disassembly
items.abstract: Introduction Intent-driven robotic disassembly requires translating operator language and noisy RGB-D perception into grounded, precedence-consistent removal plans. This work extends a perception-grounded large language model (LLM) planning framework for two-arm electric vehicle (EV) battery disassembly and evaluates the pipeline’s effectiveness after replacing the LLM backbone. Methods The system converts live RGB-D detections into structured scene text, rewrites coordinates into a frame-consistent LUZD representation, generates an ordered removal sequence, validates it with an LLM verifier, and applies a deterministic anti-hallucination filter that removes labels or coordinates not present in the perceived scene. The replacement LLM is first evaluated within the prior ensemble-based pipeline. The upgraded system then combines a single-checkpoint generator-verifier workflow, revised generator and verifier prompts, and an interactive, inspectable human-in-the-loop planning interface that displays intermediate outputs and final filtered plans. Results On the same 200-scene, 600-intent benchmark used in earlier work, mean full-list correctness was 0.824 for the prior six-sample final pipeline, 0.896 when the replacement LLM was evaluated within that prior pipeline, 0.935 with the upgraded generator alone, and 0.959 with verification and filtering. The final upgraded configuration reduced the LLM-call count from seven to two. In a 12-participant within-subject pilot, mean time to accepted answer was lower on both tasks, the mean raw NASA-TLX score was lower, and all participants preferred the new interface. Discussion These results suggest that structured scene text, clear prompts, verifier-based correction, deterministic grounding, and inspectable interfaces enhance human-in-the-loop disassembly planning.

items.title: Internet of Things-Based Physical Security Systems for Smart Cities in Saudi Arabia: A Vision 2030 Framework
items.abstract: The rapid digitalisation of cities in Saudi Arabia is leading to a greater number of connected cameras, access-control devices, environmental sensors, edge gateways and city platforms being used for the protection of people, buildings and critical infrastructure. While these systems can enhance situational awareness, they also turn physical security into a cyber-physical issue in which compromised identities, networks, analytics or actuators can have real-world effects. This review draws on peer-reviewed evidence published between 2020 and 2025 to look at how Internet of Things technologies can support physical security in Saudi smart cities while remaining resilient, privacy-conscious and operationally governable. Thirty studies verified by DOI were examined using a structured integrative approach that included topics such as smart-city security, IoT architectures, video analytics, intrusion detection, distributed trust, federated learning, digital twins, emergency response and Saudi urban governance. The synthesis highlights five interdependent capability areas: trusted sensing, edge intelligence, resilient connectivity, secure city platforms and coordinated response. It concludes that the technical effectiveness of these systems is more a matter of managing device identity, software provenance, data minimisation, model assurance, interoperability and multi-agency operating procedures than of adding more sensors. A framework aligned with Vision 2030 is suggested, focusing on risk-based zoning, zero-trust device governance, privacy-preserving analytics, resilient edge-cloud orchestration, integrated command workflows and lifecycle assurance. The framework views physical security as an adaptive public-service capability rather than as a set of separate surveillance products. The research priorities are Saudi field trials, climate-resilient sensing, common evaluation benchmarks, measuring privacy impacts and carrying out a longitudinal assessment of human-centred security outcomes.

items.title: Intersubjective resilience: Sustaining collective life under persistent life-and-death risk
items.abstract: How do organizations sustain collective life when exposure to life-and-death risk becomes a persistent condition of work? Based on an ethnographic study of two elite police units operating under continuous life-and-death risk, we find that organizations sustain coordinated collective life not by eliminating fear, resolving contradictions, or restoring stability, but by continually reorganizing these pressures into shared forms of action. We identify three interrelated organizing mechanisms. First, aspirational discipline transforms vulnerability into collective moral obligation by aligning individual striving with shared purpose. Second, paradoxical knotting enables members to act through enduring tensions, such as aggression and restraint or autonomy and obedience, without having to resolve them. Third, routine enactment restores coordinated action through recurring practices of training, reflection, and operational work. Together, these mechanisms explain how organizations maintain coherent and coordinated action when danger is an everyday condition of work. We conceptualize this capacity as intersubjective resilience : the collective accomplishment through which members repeatedly transform fear, contradiction, and disruption into coordinated action under persistent life-and-death risk.

items.title: Intrinsic and Organizational Drivers of Civil Servants' Work Motivation in Public Service Delivery: A Documentary Evidence Synthesis from Central Maluku, Indonesia
items.abstract: Civil servants' motivation is central to public-service performance, particularly in geographically dispersed local governments. This study identifies intrinsic motivational mechanisms and organizational conditions relevant to public-service delivery at the Regional Personnel and Human Resources Development Agency (BKPSDM) of Central Maluku, Indonesia. A qualitative documentary case study combined with an integrative evidence synthesis was employed. A final evidence set of 21 sources was organized into four source groups, guided by a documented search logic and eligibility protocol. Deductive and inductive coding were applied, and driver clusters were retained through three independent evidence-stream criteria: broader evidence (A), Indonesian public-sector empirical evidence (B), and direct Central Maluku/BKPSDM relevance (C). The findings show that recurrent intrinsic mechanisms include recognition and achievement, responsibility and autonomy, professional growth and competence, and public-service meaning. Organizational conditions include supervisory and organizational support, goal and administrative clarity, career development and non-financial recognition, workable administrative systems, manageable job demands, supportive working conditions, and service-user feedback. These findings suggest that motivation should be managed through a complementary architecture that links meaningful work and psychological need satisfaction with organizational resources and constraints. The documentary design provides a context-grounded framework for field testing but does not estimate employee-level causal effects.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: The study of human performance on a bicycle is not a recent phenomenon. Indeed, the cycle ergometer has been a cornerstone of physiological research for over a century, evolving from the rudimentary friction-braked devices of the late 19th century to the sophisticated laboratory instruments of today ( Vandewalle & Driss, 2015 ). This long history provided the foundation to investigate the fundamental principles of exercise physiology, many of which were first articulated by Nobel laureate A.V. Hill. His pioneering work distinguishing aerobic from anaerobic metabolism and defining concepts such as “maximum O 2 intake” established the theoretical questions that the ergometer was uniquely positioned to answer in the exercising human ( Bassett, 2002 ). The subsequent standardisation and widespread adoption of laboratory ergometry laid the groundwork for an explosion of research. In recent decades, the technological leap from stationary ergometers to mobile, on-bike power meters has coincided with a dramatic growth in scientific publications, rising from 855 in 1985 to over 18,000 in 2024 ( Figure 1.1 ).

items.title: Job rotation: A bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Job rotation is a strategic practice aimed at improving employees' health, satisfaction, and overall productivity in organizations. Its ergonomic aspects are crucial because they help balance workload, reduce ergonomic risks, and support an aging workforce. OBJECTIVE: This study addresses the lack of a field-level synthesis of job rotation research by conducting a bibliometric analysis of publications from 1994 through 2025, with particular attention to ergonomic themes, trends, and relationships in the literature. METHODS: A bibliometric analysis was conducted using 820 records retrieved from Scopus. VOSviewer was used to examine keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship, author bibliographic coupling, title-and-abstract term co-occurrence, and author co-citation networks. RESULTS: The analysis shows rapid growth in the literature on job rotation and its critical components. The visualizations show the evolution of research topics and their interrelationships. The mapped literature emphasizes ergonomic and organizational themes including workload balancing, musculoskeletal risk, work design, scheduling, worker well-being, and job satisfaction. CONCLUSIONS: The study underlines the increasing emphasis on the ergonomic and organizational benefits of job rotation. It proposes conducting further research to address existing gaps and promote employee well-being and productivity through effective job rotation strategies.

items.title: Knowledge Sharing and Organizational Performance: A Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis of Mechanisms, Contexts and Outcomes (2014-2025)
items.abstract: Purpose: This review explains how knowledge sharing is converted into organizational performance and identifies the organizational, technological and contextual conditions that enable, constrain or redirect this conversion. Design/methodology/approach: A systematic literature review covering 2014-2025 was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and management-review guidance. The final analytical corpus comprises 92 empirical studies: 46 published during 2014-2024 and 46 published in 2025. The 2014-2024 screening sequence reported in the manuscript began with 1,204 records, of which 912 remained after deduplication; 96 were assessed in full text and 46 were retained. For 2025, 75 records were identified; after removal of duplicates/overlaps, one out-of-period record and two retracted reports, 67 were assessed and 46 retained. Eligibility, extraction and thematic coding were conducted by a single primary reviewer using explicit criteria, an audit trail and repeated coding. The synthesis combined descriptive mapping with iterative thematic analysis; no meta-analysis was conducted because constructs, outcome levels and effect statistics were heterogeneous. Findings: Across the 2014-2025 literature, five interdependent themes emerged: enabling and inhibiting conditions; forms and quality of knowledge sharing; conversion mechanisms; multidimensional performance outcomes; and boundary conditions. The evidence is consistent with a conditional conversion pathway in which culture, trust, leadership, support, structure and digital infrastructure shape exchange, while learning, innovation, improvisation, agility, ambidexterity, knowledge quality and application help explain how sharing is associated with performance. The 2025 subset places stronger emphasis on artificial intelligence, human-machine interaction, knowledge-sharing quality, sustainability and the balance between sharing and protection. This late-period concentration is interpreted as an emerging development rather than a definitive temporal break. Mixed and non-significant findings show that more sharing is not automatically better. Research limitations/implications: The evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional, self-reported SEM studies and emerging-economy contexts. A single-reviewer process and heterogeneous outcome measures limit causal and statistical generalization. Practical implications: Managers should manage the complete conversion chain: identify strategically relevant knowledge, create safe and well-governed sharing channels, validate quality, embed application in work processes and evaluate proximal and distal performance outcomes. Originality/value: The review extends earlier enabler-process-outcome syntheses by isolating the knowledge-sharing-to-performance pathway, separating proximal from distal performance outcomes, incorporating boundary conditions and failure paths, and proposing a dynamic conversion framework that integrates AI, knowledge quality, ambidexterity and governance. It also distinguishes established themes across the review period from emerging emphases concentrated in the 2025 subset.
