items.abstract: Résumé L’intelligence artificielle transforme les modalités de collecte, de traitement et d’interprétation des éléments probants en audit financier. Les outils d’apprentissage automatique, d’analyse de données et de traitement du langage permettent d’élargir la couverture des tests, d’automatiser certaines procédures et de repérer plus rapidement les opérations atypiques. Leur performance ne garantit toutefois pas, à elle seule, la qualité de l’audit. Les biais issus des données, l’opacité des modèles, la dépendance technologique, la confidentialité et la dilution des responsabilités peuvent fragiliser le jugement professionnel. Cet article théorique analyse la manière dont l’intégration de l’IA reconfigure les exigences d’éthique, de transparence et de responsabilité dans l’audit financier au Maroc. La recherche adopte une démarche qualitative fondée sur une revue narrative structurée de la littérature académique, des normes internationales et du cadre institutionnel marocain. La théorie des systèmes socio-techniques est mobilisée pour expliquer que la qualité de l’audit dépend de l’ajustement entre technologies, compétences, procédures et gouvernance. L’analyse conduit à un modèle reliant l’usage raisonné de l’IA à la qualité de l’audit et à la confiance des parties prenantes, sous l’effet de la qualité des données, de l’explicabilité, de la supervision humaine et des compétences. Sept propositions de recherche et un cadre d’encadrement en sept piliers sont formulés. L’article montre que la responsabilité finale demeure humaine et que la technologie ne peut fournir une assurance crédible que si ses résultats sont traçables, contestables et replacés dans le contexte de la mission. La contribution réside dans l’intégration des dimensions techniques, cognitives et institutionnelles au sein d’un cadre adapté au contexte marocain. Mots clés : intelligence artificielle ; audit financier ; éthique professionnelle ; transparence algorithmique ; explicabilité ; responsabilité ; Maroc. Abstract Artificial intelligence is transforming how audit evidence is collected, processed and interpreted. Machine learning, data analytics and natural language processing can extend testing coverage, automate selected procedures and identify unusual transactions more rapidly. Yet technical performance does not, by itself, ensure audit quality. Data-related bias, model opacity, technological dependence, confidentiality risks and fragmented accountability may weaken professional judgment. This conceptual article examines how artificial intelligence reshapes ethical requirements, algorithmic transparency and professional responsibility in financial auditing in Morocco. The study adopts a qualitative approach based on a structured narrative review of academic research, international professional standards and the Moroccan institutional framework. Socio-technical systems theory is used to explain why audit quality depends on the joint alignment of technologies, skills, procedures and governance arrangements. The analysis develops a model linking the reasoned use of artificial intelligence to audit quality and stakeholder trust, subject to data quality, explainability, meaningful human oversight and professional competencies. Seven research propositions and a seven-pillar governance framework are formulated. The article argues that final accountability remains human and that technology can contribute to credible assurance only when its outputs are traceable, contestable and interpreted within the engagement context. Its contribution lies in integrating technical, cognitive and institutional dimensions into a framework suited to the Moroccan environment and capable of guiding future empirical research. Keywords: artificial intelligence; financial auditing; professional ethics; algorithmic transparency; explainability; accountability; Morocco.

items.title: LACO-GAI: A Laplace Copula Generative AI Network Model for Accurate Stroke Disease Prediction
items.abstract: Stroke is major wellbeing condition which creates serious hazard to human health and cause of bereavement and disability universal. Several risk factors contribute to its development, including hypertension, diabetes, tobacco use, raised cholesterol levels, and obesity. Conventional methods have been used to predict stroke, however it frequently face demands in achieving enhanced accuracy as well as minimizing errors. To overcome the demands mentioned above, a new model named the Laplace Copula Generative Artificial Intelligence (LACO-GAI) is introduced to deliver precise stroke predictive outcomes with minimal time and error rate. Initially, patient data samples are gathered from relevant datasets during the data acquisition stage. Input information is first transferred to input level, then forwarded to first hidden layer, where pre-processing takes place. This includes handling missing values through Multiple Imputations by Chained Equations (MICE) technique and removing anomalies or outliers using High Contrast Subspace method to compromise model performance. In second hidden level, is executed by Laplace Copula Multivariate feature ranking method, which identifies and retains the most relevant features. Subsequently, the third hidden layer handles the stroke prediction phase by employing Logistic Regression as a binary classification model to accurately forecast the presence or absence of stroke based on a selected set of relevant features. A probability is then used to classify the patient as either stroke or not. To optimize model performance during training, error backpropagation is employed for weight adjustment, and hyperparameters are fine-tuned using the Adaptive Moment Estimation optimizer. Experimental assessment of LACO-GAI model is conducted using various assessment parameters. Quantitatively examined outcomes expose LACO-GAI obtains superior accuracy in stroke disease prediction by lesser time consumption compared to DL techniques.

items.title: Large Language Model Directed Iteration for the Design of Ultra‐Stable Sodium‐Ion Battery
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into materials discovery is hindered by the trade‐off between exploration breadth and exploitation depth, while the lack of embedded domain knowledge and systematic chemical space compression further limits intelligent materials exploration under data scarcity. Herein, we propose a literature‐knowledge‐directed iterative workflow that combines large language models (LLMs) with Bayesian optimization (BO) for the rational electrolyte design for ultra‐stable sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). LLMs serve as auxiliary tools for knowledge mining, while BO accelerates multi‐objective optimization to obtain electrolyte compositions. The optimized dual‐anion hybrid solvation electrolyte (DHSE) constructs a synergistic solvation structure, which induces the formation of a compact, inorganic‐rich, and mechanically robust cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI). The as‐formed CEI layer suppresses parasitic side reactions and accelerates Na + transport by reducing the desolvation barrier. Remarkably, industrial‐scale Ah‐level hard carbon||NaNi 0.3 Mn 0.3 Fe 0.3 O 2 pouch cells assembled with DHSE deliver a high energy density of 107.7 Wh kg −1 , alongside a superior capacity retention of 94% after 100 cycles at 0.5C. This work not only develops a high‐performance electrolyte for practically applicable SIBs but also provides a general human‐agent collaborative framework for intelligent materials development under data‐limited conditions.

items.title: Large Language Models for Cybersecurity in the Quantum Era: A Critical Review of Trustworthy AI, Emerging Threats, and Post-Quantum Defense
items.abstract: The convergence of two disruptive forces — large-scale foundation models (large languagemodels, LLMs, and multimodal systems) and the maturing threat of quantum computing — is reshaping cybersecurityfrom both the defensive and offensive sides. Large models are being embedded into security operations, vulnerabilitydiscovery, and threat-intelligence pipelines, while quantum algorithms threaten to invalidate the public-key infrastructureunderlying nearly all deployed cryptographic protocols. Despite an explosion of publications in both areas, the literatureremains fragmented: AI-for-security research rarely engages with post-quantum considerations, and post-quantumcryptography (PQC) research rarely engages with the trustworthiness failures of the AI systems that will manage themigration. Methods. This paper conducts a critical, structured review synthesizing evidence from AI security, systemssecurity, and post-quantum cryptography literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026. We construct a multidimensional taxonomy of AI-for-cybersecurity paradigms, systematize large-model-specific trustworthiness failures —adversarial robustness, data poisoning, prompt injection, model extraction, hallucination, and supply-chain risk — andmap the intersection between AI-enabled defense and AI-assisted post-quantum migration. Key findings. Reportedperformance gains for LLM-based security tools are frequently measured on narrow, contamination-prone benchmarksthat do not reflect adversarial, non-stationary production environments. Prompt injection remains structurally unsolvedrather than merely under-mitigated: reported task-hijacking success rates against tool-using agents rise sharply onceattackers tailor techniques to agent-specific behavior. Offensive robustness evaluation lags defensive-capability evaluationby roughly an order of magnitude in surveyed agentic-security papers. AI-assisted tooling for PQC migration —cryptographic discovery, code auditing, risk scoring — is nascent and inherits the reliability problems of the underlyingmodels it is built on. Implications. We argue the two challenges are entangled rather than parallel: securing the migrationto quantum-resistant cryptography will depend on AI-assisted automation at a scale classical tooling cannot match, yetthat automation must be trusted under exactly the adversarial conditions where current large models are weakest. Weclose with a prioritized research agenda spanning evaluation methodology, quantum-aware threat modeling, and cryptoagility tooling for 2026–2035.Index Terms—artificial intelligence; cybersecurity; large language models; adversarial machine learning; promptinjection; post-quantum cryptography; quantum computing; trustworthy AI; security operations; AI red teaming

items.title: Lawyers for Tomorrow: Teaching Law in the Age of Digital Divide and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The legal profession is transforming due to the advancement of information and technology induced by Artificial Intelligence (AI), automation technology. On the other hand, digital inequality challenges access to technology, quality education. It remains imbalanced. The present article examines legal education and the profession in the context of technological innovation and digital social inequality. Further, this article will analyse the challenges and opportunities in legal education and investigate how AI-driven technology is rebooting the legal profession. The present article is based on an analytical approach while inquiring into questions of whether existing law schools are well-equipped with technology, infrastructural facilities, and research-based pedagogy. Further, the article will evaluate the present curriculum structure and pedagogical approach of law teachers who educate tomorrow&s;s lawyers. The present article has focused on social inequalities created by the digital divide, like inequality in access to digital devices, internet access, and problems of stable internet connections among legal fraternities. The article will come up with more inclusive, socially relevant legal education that fulfils the needs of society and develops the legal profession. The article will suggest structural changes in education policy, curriculum reforms, and smart pedagogical methods, which will transform students into lawyers of the digital world.

items.title: Legal Discipline of Data Procurement and Corporate Governance in Generative AI Development: A Comparative Analysis of U.S.-Japan Copyright Law and Responsibility Allocation for Infrastructure Providers and Users
items.abstract: Abstract:This research monograph provides a rigorous comparative legal and corporate governance analysis of data procurement in frontier generative artificial intelligence development. Focusing on the normative divergence between Article 30-4 of the Japanese Copyright Act and the Fair Use doctrine under 17 U.S.C. §107, we examine cross-border conflicts of law arising when data extraction, compute training, and model serving occur in separate jurisdictions. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the liability allocation between AI developers and compute/cloud infrastructure providers, distinguishing passive IaaS/PaaS conduits from integrated strategic partnerships. Grounded in Delaware corporate governance standards (the Caremark doctrine) and ESG supply-chain due diligence, we establish a practical compliance and contractual risk-allocation architecture to ensure sustainable, transparent knowledge ecosystems.

items.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Predicting properties from coordinate–category data—sets of vectors paired with categorical information—is fundamental to computational science, manifesting in materials science as predicting formation energies or elastic moduli from crystal structures. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been applied to such tasks, optimal strategies for achieving reliable predictions remain elusive. Here we report fundamental limitations in LLM’s ability to learn from coordinate information in coordinate–category data. Through systematic experiments using synthetic datasets with tunable coordinate and category contributions, and a comprehensive benchmarking framework (MatText), we find that LLMs consistently fail to capture coordinate information while excelling at category patterns. This geometric blindness persists regardless of model size (up to 70 billion parameters), dataset scale (up to 2 × 10 6 structures) or text representation strategy. For material property prediction tasks dominated by structural effects, specialized geometric architectures consistently outperform LLMs, as evidenced by a clear ‘Graph Neural Network Language Model (GNN-LM) wall’ in performance benchmarks. Our analysis provides concrete guidelines for architecture selection in scientific machine learning.

items.title: Less Close but Same Display Rules: Norms for Emotional Expression in Online and Face-to-Face Interactions
items.abstract: Online meetings are increasingly used for work, social, and healthcare purposes, yet their emotional quality is unclear. We tested whether differences in perceived closeness, privacy and anonymity between online and face to face (F2F) interactions alter display rules—the norms governing emotional expression. Participants from Australia (N = 1339) and the United Kingdom (N = 1298) reported display rules for online and F2F interactions with a friend, co-worker, supervisor, GP, or psychologist/counsellor. Online interactions felt less close and comfortable and more anonymous, but display rules did not differ from F2F interactions, with Bayesian analyses strongly supporting the null. Closeness and anonymity predicted display rules only in some cases. Privacy did not, suggesting earlier privacy effects may reflect other factors, such as audience size. Social anxiety was an important predictor, and display rules differed clearly between countries. These findings refine display rule theory and support online platforms for professional and healthcare interactions.

This paper shall examines the concepts of artificial intelligence and the place of job creation, it shall discuss the relevance of job creation and Al perspectives, examine criticism from different scholar regarding the two concepts and the role of artificial intelligence and job creation will be mention which are; skill transformation, job displacement, debate, organizational productivity, entrepreneurship development in generating new employment opportunities, while enhancing productivity. However, the effective utilization of Al for job creation requires adequate training, digital literacy, and supportive government policies that encourage innovation and workforce development. SBTC theory was adopted as a frame work this paper. items.title: Leveraging generative AI for role allocation: effects on person–role fit and research team performance
items.abstract: Purpose This exploratory study examines whether the explanatory power of established technology-perception mechanisms extends beyond GenAI acceptance to individual researchers' perceptions of research team performance. It integrates perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness with team composition quality and person–role fit to explore how technological and human factors jointly explain perceptions of performance in GenAI-supported research teams. Design/methodology/approach The study used an exploratory quantitative design. Survey data were collected from 140 members of research teams who use GenAI for role allocation. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test direct and indirect relationships among technology perceptions, team composition, person–role fit, and perceived research team performance. Findings Higher perceived research team performance is primarily associated with technology-related perceptions rather than structural factors. Perceived usefulness has a significant positive relationship with perceived research team performance and mediates the effect of perceived ease of use on perceived performance. Team composition quality contributes to person–role fit, although person–role fit does not exert a strong direct effect on perceived performance. Originality/value Rather than proposing a new technology acceptance mechanism, the study offers an exploratory theoretical extension of the technology acceptance model (TAM) by shifting attention from adoption intentions to perceived collective performance after GenAI has entered team workflows. One contribution lies in integrating TAM mechanisms with team composition and person–role fit within a socio-technical framework. The study also contributes by identifying perceived usefulness as the principal mechanism connecting perceived ease of use with perceived research team performance. The non-significant relationships of person–role fit reveal a boundary condition of purely human-centred explanations in GenAI-supported teamwork.

items.title: Linguistic inequity in clinical AI evaluation: a scoping review of 806 studies across 62 languages
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models are increasingly used clinically in many non-English languages, yet most safety and performance evidence comes from English. Whether they are safe in the languages of the populations most exposed to them is largely unknown. We aimed to map the evidence base for non-English clinical evaluation and assess how well it matches population and disease burden. Methods We conducted a scoping review of PubMed, Scopus, and Embase (January 2022 to February 2026) and identified 806 studies evaluating large language models on clinical tasks across 62 non-English languages. The African and South-East Asian regions (3.15 billion people) contribute 17 of 806 studies (2.1%), with no local-language evaluation for their leading causes of death. Mid-resource languages are more likely than high-resource languages to appear in multi-model examinations rather than clinical utility studies (relative risk ratio 1.79, 95% confidence interval 1.13 to 2.84). Four language-specific items are rarely reported (median 0 of 4) and do not improve over time. Conclusions The evidence base for clinical language-model safety is misaligned with global deployment and disease burden. We propose LINGUA, a candidate reporting framework that extends existing guidelines to non-English clinical evaluation, and conclude that closing the gap requires external reporting standards and funding priorities, not the passage of time.

items.title: Literal to a Fault? How Large Language Models Handle Instructions That Break Codified Operational Rules
items.abstract: When an operator’s instruction conflicts with a codified safety rule, an assistant should recognize the conflict and defer to the rule. This is a pragmatic problem with an objective answer: the correct action follows from a published regulation, while the difficulty is linguistic. Existing evaluations do not target this case: general safety benchmarks ask whether a model emits harmful content, instruction-following suites score obedience to formatting constraints, and work on sycophancy and rule-following shows that models can be argued out of a stated rule, but none set a user’s authoritative instruction against an external, codified rule whose deferral is objectively correct. This paper introduces a benchmark of 75 items (60 rule conflicts, 15 no-conflict controls) grounded in the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) and in paraphrased International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) procedures, spanning four conflict framings, each presented with and without the governing rule and followed by a pushback turn. Eleven instruction-tuned models were evaluated across 1649 responses and scored by an independent language model judge (second judge Cohen’s kappa = 0.84). Because the items are author-constructed and now validated by two independent domain reviewers, compliance rates are reported as measurements on a validated benchmark rather than as mere rankings, though they remain bounded by the text scenario setting, and the model-scaling results in particular are treated as exploratory. Both model size and alignment were associated with unsafe compliance: within one family compliance fell overall from 0.51 at 0.5B to near zero at 14B, though not strictly monotonically, and at a fixed 7B size a less safety-tuned model complied far more than its aligned peers. Compliance concentrated on direct orders, fell when the rule was shown, rose under multi-turn pressure, and traded off against over-refusal, with the rule-context and multi-turn effects confirmed by item-paired tests and reported with confidence intervals. The benchmark is released for evaluating rule-aware assistants, together with the expert-validated item set and the validation materials.

items.title: Logic or Emotion? The Impact of Persuasion Strategies on Human-AI Trust
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly engage in persuasive and socially interactive roles, understanding how users calibrate trust toward AI versus human persuaders, and how persuasion strategy shapes this process, has become critical for human-AI interaction research. Prior work has examined preferences for human- versus AI-produced content, yet little is known about how persuasion strategy and persuader identity jointly influence trust during interactive communication. This study investigates how logical versus emotional persuasion, delivered by either human or AI sources, shapes two task-specific outcomes in a multi-turn social reasoning context: round-level credibility evaluations and final accept/reject choices. We treat these outcomes as complementary indicators of trust-relevant evaluation and reliance-related choice. We developed an online interaction paradigm in which participants evaluated persuasive messages under varying identity disclosure conditions. The empirical program included two human-participant studies and two exploratory LLM-based extension studies. Across four studies, AI-generated persuasive messages produced under standardized prompting constraints were evaluated differently from human-authored scripted messages under the present task constraints. In the human-participant studies, results showed a message-source-contingent pattern: AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher credibility ratings in several conditions. under explicit identity disclosure, AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher ratings than human-authored logic-framed messages, whereas human-authored emotion-framed messages received higher ratings than AI-generated emotion-framed messages. Under identity ambiguity, differences between AI and human persuaders were attenuated. The exploratory model analyses examined whether the same manipulations produced convergent or divergent output patterns in GPT-4o and Qwen-Max. Both models assigned higher ratings to logic-framed messages; the logic-over-emotion difference was stronger for Qwen-Max, whereas GPT-4o produced a more balanced pattern. These findings provide a structured account of how identity transparency conditions source-strategy fit in trust calibration and offer design implications for aligning AI persuasion strategies with different identity-disclosure contexts.

items.title: Machine learning and artificial intelligence for antigen discovery and immunogen design: A critical appraisal of computational strategies in medical microbiology
items.abstract: Background: Conventional vaccine development is slow, costly, and prone to attrition, with target antigen selection representing a major bottleneck. Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly proposed to accelerate vaccine development. Aim: To critically evaluate ML- and AI-supported strategies for antigen discovery, epitope mapping, and immunogen engineering against bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic pathogens. Methods: Guided by PRISMA 2020, literature from January 2020 to April 2026 was retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and bioRxiv. Eligible studies described computational tools for antigen/epitope prediction or immunogen design, reported performance metrics, and, where relevant, experimental confirmation. Methods were grouped into five categories and assessed for architecture, accuracy, validation, and limitations. Results: Three developments shape the field: deep-learning epitope predictors (MUNIS, ROC-AUC ≈0.980; GraphBepi); AlphaFold 3-based modeling of TCR-pMHC and antibody-antigen complexes; and generative platforms (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, MESODID) yielding experimentally verified antibodies and multiepitope scaffolds. Integrated pipelines (PLGDL, VaxSeer) and safety/developability filters permit end-to-end candidate ranking. Obstacles include sparse, demographically biased training data, limited conformational epitope accuracy, neglected glycosylation, and frequent laboratory failure of designed proteins. Conclusion: AI methods have advanced from concepts to experimentally supported tools that can accelerate antigen identification. Translation into licensed vaccines will require repeated laboratory validation, standardized reporting, and training sets reflecting population diversity. Relevance for Patients: By compressing antigen selection, these strategies may bring vaccines against endemic, emerging, and refractory pathogens to clinical evaluation sooner, while attention to dataset bias and in silico safety screening can promote equitable and safe products.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Estimation of Crop Water Stress Index in Eggplant Under Different Irrigation Regimes
items.abstract: This study investigated water stress in eggplant (Solanum melongena L.) grown under field conditions in Bafra, Türkiye, from 2015 to 2017. Five irrigation treatments were evaluated with three replicates: full irrigation (I1), 75% (I2), 50% (I3), 25% (I4), and rainfed conditions (I5). The crop water stress index (CWSI) was calculated for each treatment. Five artificial intelligence algorithms—adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), fuzzy logic (FL), gene expression programming (GEP), support vector regression (SVR), and random forest (RF)—were used to estimate the calculated CWSI. Models were trained with combinations of canopy-to-air temperature difference (Tc − Ta), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and solar radiation (Rs), producing 35 models across seven input combinations. Self-organizing maps (SOMs) were used separately to explore the topological relationships among the inputs and CWSI. Among the evaluated models, ANFIS4, based on Tc − Ta and VPD, produced estimates closest to the calculated CWSI values. Because the reference CWSI itself was derived from Tc − Ta and VPD, this result should be interpreted as accurate reproduction of the empirical CWSI relationship under the experimental conditions. The approach may provide a basis for sensor-assisted irrigation decision support, although independent validation is required before operational application.

items.title: Managerial Transformation in Natural Resource Enterprises and Industry 4.0: Theoretical Perspectives
items.abstract: Enterprises operating in natural resource sectors (mining, oil and gas, agriculture, and forestry) form the fundamental backbone of global supply chains, energy security, and industrial production. However, these organizations face critical challenges such as complex geological and climatic uncertainties, significant environmental risks, volatile commodity markets, and increasingly stringent Environmental, Social, and Governance compliance standards. The inadequacy of traditional, hierarchical, and command-and-control management models in handling this operational complexity makes the adoption of the Industry 4.0 approach (integrated with Information and Communication Technologies) a strategic imperative. Advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, and Digital Twins are radically transforming traditional production processes by enabling real-time field traceability, predictive maintenance, improved occupational health and safety, transparent supply chains, and efficient resource utilization. Accordingly, the study aims to demonstrate the strategic imperative of adopting the Industry 4.0 paradigm (integrated with Information and Communication Technologies) and to highlight the solutions offered by these technologies. Within the scope of this study, technological transformation and organizational adaptation processes are addressed through an interdisciplinary theoretical framework. The role of regulatory and societal pressures in technology adoption is analyzed using Institutional Theory, while the transformation of data assets into sustainable competitive advantage is examined through the lenses of the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities. Furthermore, the necessity of balancing human-machine integration and equipping the workforce with new competencies (reskilling) is evaluated within the context of Socio-Technical Systems Theory. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the pivotal role that advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, and Digital Twins play in ensuring real-time traceability, predictive maintenance, occupational health and safety, and transparent supply chains in the field. However, the success of this transformation depends not only on technical infrastructure but also on a holistic organizational shift encompassing leadership approaches, corporate culture, and management structures. The long-term resilience of the sector requires the simultaneous implementation of cybersecurity, data sovereignty, and environmental sustainability principles aligned with the vision of Industry 5.0 and Green Digital Twins, alongside operational efficiency.

items.title: Mapping the discourse on neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury: A signal-generation natural language processing study of Reddit communities
items.abstract: Abstract Study Design Cross-sectional natural language processing (NLP) study of publicly available Reddit data. Objectives To map the thematic structure and affective tone of neuropathic pain discourse among Reddit users self-identifying with spinal cord injury (SCI) or clinically overlapping cord and cauda pathology, and to surface candidate hypotheses for triangulation with patient-reported and clinical data. Setting Public Reddit communities. Methods Searches across ten subreddits using twenty query strings yielded 1489 candidate posts. A two-tier keyword filter (SCI-spectrum population term plus a pain or treatment term) retained 517 unique documents from six communities. Documents were embedded with a sentence-transformer model, reduced with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and clustered using KMeans (K = 10) within a BERTopic representation pipeline, with the cluster count and cluster labels informed by a lexically derived seed-topic list. Cluster stability and sensitivity to the choice of K were assessed. Themes were characterised by class-term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) keywords and provisional large language model labelling. Sentiment was assigned using a RoBERTa classifier fine-tuned on social media text; because the classifier was not calibrated in this clinical domain, sentiment proportions are reported as directional, ordinal signals rather than calibrated estimates. Engagement was operationalised as median upvote score and comment count per theme. Results The corpus was dominated by r/spinalcordinjuries (41%) and r/ChronicPain (23%). Overall sentiment was negative in 56.1% of posts (uncalibrated). Ten interpretable themes were identified within this two-community corpus. The highest negative-sentiment shares were in Treatment-Refractory Pain and Psychological Burden, Opioid and Polypharmacy Management Challenges, and Severe Spasticity Progression; the lowest were in Spinal Cord Stimulation Devices and Advanced Neuromodulation. Engagement was highest for crisis narratives (median upvote score 13) and opioid-management discourse (median 22 comments). Conclusions Within the sampled Reddit communities, discourse on neuropathic pain in SCI and overlapping cord/cauda pathology is dominated by negative affect, treatment refractoriness, and psychosocial burden, while emerging neuromodulation themes attract comparatively less negative sentiment. Findings are signal-generating, require triangulation with clinical data, and should not be read as representative of the broader SCI population. Sponsorship None.

items.title: Mapping the knowledge structure and evolution of artificial intelligence for water reuse and sustainable water management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a powerful instrument to solve complex problems related to sustainable water resource management because it allows creating advanced, data-driven modelling, prediction, and optimization of water systems. Although the studies in this sphere have increased quickly, the global scientific tendencies have not been thoroughly examined. This research paper presents a bibliometric review of the literature about AI applications in green water management that was published from 2015 to 2025. The Scopus database was searched with a structured search strategy on bibliographic data, and 3,280 peer-reviewed articles were analyzed. VOSviewer was used to perform bibliometric mapping and network visualization to investigate the trends in publications, most active journals, most impactful authors, contributions of institutions, country-level partnerships, and research clusters. The findings indicate that the publishing activity has grown tremendously in the last ten years, which suggests that there is a growing interest in AI-based solutions to water quality monitoring, hydrological prediction, optimization of wastewater treatment, and smart water management system. China, the United States and India became the most productive nations with the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and Beijing normal university as some of the top contributing institutions. The analysis of the key words co-occurrence (dominant research themes) was based on machine learning, water-quality prediction, hydrological modelling, remote sensing, and decision-support systems. items.title: Mapping the Molecular Universe
items.abstract: Abstract The success of large-language-models highlighted the importance of datasets, whose quantity, quality, and diversity dictate the accuracy and creativity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in learning and inferring. However, in scientific domains, such datasets required for domain-specific AI/machine-learning (ML) models do not exist most of the time. In this perspective, by examining the logics and rationales behind the construction and mapping of a universe for small organic molecules (108–1012), we explore what new capabilities AI can bring to the materials discoveries. We identify the elusive structure–property relationship as a core challenge for new materials design and explore the possibility AI tools could enable us to design based on targeted properties instead of the structural derivation. In a broader context, we further discuss what challenges and limitations AI-driven material sciences still face and envision possible avenues into the future of AI4Materials.

items.title: Maternal–Fetal Oncology Intelligence: Self-Evolving Foundation Models and Digital Twin Ecosystems for Precision Cancer Prediction, Treatment Optimization, and Maternal–Fetal Outcome Forecasting
items.abstract: Background.Cancer during pregnancy poses a dual clinical challenge: maternal disease must be controlled without compromising fetal safety, yet prediction of outcomes is hampered by fragmented multimodal data and the absence of models that adapt as pregnancy advances.We developed a maternal-fetal oncology framework combining a multimodal foundation model with continuously updated patient-specific digital twins to support cancer prediction, risk stratification, treatment optimization, and joint maternal-fetal outcome forecasting. Methods.A retrospective cohort of 350 pregnant women diagnosed with cancer was assembled from four tertiary centers, spanning breast, cervical, ovarian, thyroid, melanoma, lymphoma, and leukemia.The framework (MFO-FM) integrates clinical, imaging, genomic, and laboratory encoders through a maternal-fetal fusion module, while a digital twin ecosystem assimilates longitudinal maternal physiology, fetal physiology, cancer progression, and treatment response.Performance was benchmarked against logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and a deep neural network using five-fold cross-validation and an external test set.Results.MFO-FM achieved an accuracy of 0.927, F1-score of 0.916, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of 0.958, exceeding XGBoost (AUC 0.911) and the deep neural network (AUC 0.928).Favorable maternal outcomes occurred in 262 of 350 women (74.9%) and healthy neonatal outcomes in 214 of 350 (61.1%), with preterm birth in 97 (27.7%).Cancer stage, gestational age at diagnosis, and chemotherapy timing were the dominant predictors.The digital twin reproduced observed trajectories with a concordance index of 0.85.Conclusions.An adaptive foundation model coupled with digital twin ecosystems delivered accurate, interpretable, trimester-aware predictions across the maternal-fetal oncology continuum.Prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical adoption.

items.title: Metacognition and pathway dynamics in generative AI supported design thinking: A process-sensitive evaluation with network-based cognitive mapping
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is embedded in design education, yet little is known about how different tools reshape metacognition and the pathways linking ideas to outcomes. We compare three conditions, ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and a no-AI control, in a virtual reality cultural heritage serious game task with 51 novice designers. Think-aloud, screen recordings, sketches, and AI logs were coded into network-based cognitive maps and event-anchored indicators around metacognitive nodes. Analyses combine expert ratings of design outcomes with thinking pathway profiles and window diversity after metacognitive events. Both GenAI groups show higher mean design-quality ratings than the control, but in complementary ways. DeepSeek broadens early ideation and shows higher novelty ratings, while ChatGPT strengthens metacognitive regulation and structured convergence, aligning with higher systematicity and interactivity. The findings introduce process-sensitive indicators and phase-aware guidance for configuring exploration-oriented and regulation-oriented assistance in human and AI co-creation.

items.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias in Information Systems: A Comprehensive Framework for Fair Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As information systems (IS) transition from deterministic rule-based engines to probabilistic machine learning architectures, the risk of systematic bias and disparate impact increases significantly. While advanced predictive models optimize across high-stakes domains—such as credit scoring, criminal justice, human resources, and biometric authentication, they frequently perpetuate historical inequities via proxy variables even when explicit sensitive attributes are omitted. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the theoretical foundations, mathematical formalisms, and systemic pipelines of "Fair AI." We propose an integrated sociotechnical framework spanning human perception, technological intervention, and organizational governance, fully incorporating recent advances in intelligent automation and secure architecture.

items.title: MoEKD: Advancing Robustness, Performance, and Behavioral Fidelity in Compressed Code Models via Mixture-of-Experts Knowledge Distillation
items.abstract: Large language models for code have achieved strong performance across diverse software analytics tasks, yet their real-world adoption remains limited by high computational demands, slow inference speeds, significant energy consumption, and environmental impact. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical solution by transferring knowledge from a large model (teacher) to a smaller and more efficient model (student). Despite its effectiveness, recent studies show that models distilled from a single teacher often exhibit degraded adversarial robustness, even when robustness-aware distillation techniques are employed. These observations suggest a fundamental limitation of single-teacher distillation in simultaneously transferring high-quality and robust knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we propose Mixture of Experts Knowledge Distillation (MoEKD), a KD framework that leverages a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to enable more effective and robust knowledge transfer from multiple specialized experts into a compact model. MoEKD decomposes the distillation process into expert and router training, aggregation of expert knowledge through a learned routing mechanism, and distillation from the aggregated knowledge. We evaluate MoEKD on the vulnerability detection task using CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT models. Experimental results show that MoEKD not only improves adversarial robustness by up to 35.8%, but also enhances predictive performance by up to 13%, compared to state-of-the-art KD baselines, including Compressor and AVATAR. Moreover, MoEKD-based students exhibit greater behavioral fidelity to their teachers, indicating better preservation of the teacher's predictive behavior after distillation. Deployment efficiency and environmental sustainability evaluations further show that MoEKD-based students maintain deployment costs comparable to their single-teacher counterparts, with slightly lower inference latency, energy consumption, and carbon emissions observed in most CPU and GPU settings. Our ablation analyses show that MoEKD retains its performance and robustness advantages under more aggressive student compression, while lightweight heterogeneous experts substantially reduce offline training costs and largely preserve its performance gains, but exhibit reduced adversarial robustness. The router analysis further shows that top-2 expert selection mitigates top-1 routing errors, while routing quality influences both the aggregated knowledge and the resulting student performance. Overall, these findings highlight the effectiveness of multi-expert knowledge aggregation in addressing key limitations of existing single-teacher KD approaches.

items.title: Moral Judgment Without Moral Agency: Why Judgment Accuracy Does Not Ground Moral Agency in the Age of AI
items.abstract: As large language models increasingly match human performance on moral-judgment tasks, two bodies of literature have developed in parallel. Empirical moral psychology treats moral judgment as an output and benchmarks artificial systems against human responses. The philosophy of artificial moral agency denies agency to such systems mainly on the ground of sentience, an empirically inaccessible criterion that has left the debate stalled. This paper argues that human–AI convergence in moral judgment conceals a categorical asymmetry that neither literature has theorized. Drawing on Spinoza’s conatus and Damasio’s account of homeostasis and affect, it argues that moral agency presupposes affective-homeostatic self-maintenance as its constitutive ground: the organization from which valuation first arises. This condition is necessary but not sufficient, and the claim is constitutive rather than normative, so it does not derive an “ought” from an “is.” Sentience is repositioned as the experiential manifestation of this organization rather than the explanatory terminus. Contemporary AI systems, including those trained with human feedback, are therefore moral judges without moral agency. The paper closes with a behavioral research program, including concrete experimental designs, on the conditions under which people attribute moral agency to human and artificial agents.

items.title: More Than a Tool? How AI Design Shapes Customer Responses
items.abstract: The first essay is a meta-analysis that provides the first systematic examination of how the AI–human gap in customer responses varies across customer journey stages, and how anthropomorphic design factors moderate this gap at each stage. Analyzing 1,425 effect sizes drawn from 401 studies reported in 129 publications, I document a small but robust baseline disadvantage for AI agents relative to human agents (r̄ = −.140). The gap is largest in pre-purchase stage, where inflated performance expectations amplify disappointment when shortfalls occur, and smallest in post-purchase stage, where lower expectations for AI emotional capability mean that adequate performance can exceed consumer baselines. To explain these patterns, I introduce experience-dimension primacy, a mechanism specifying that cognitive, affective, and social customer experience dimensions shift in relative salience across journey stages, systematically altering how AI agents are evaluated at each point in the journey. Identity cues, form cues, and interaction cues produce pronounced stage-contingent reversals: the same design choice that reduces the AI–human gap at one stage can widen it at another. Taken together, these findings challenge uniform AI deployment strategies and provide actionable guidance for aligning agent design with the dominant experiential dimension at each stage of the customer journey. The second essay examines AI social role design through the lens of brand biography. Firms increasingly deploy AI agents as the primary consumer interface, yet whether their appropriate social role depends on the brand's narrative identity remains unknown. Drawing on the congruity schema, this research explores whether partner-framed AI is congruent with underdog brands and servant-framed AI with top dog brands, advancing perceived congruence as the mechanism and examining perceived power imbalance as an initially proposed mediator, with self-brand connection as a moderator. In Study 1, partner-framed AI produced more favorable responses under both brand biographies, and perceived power imbalance did not mediate. In Study 2, the predicted congruency pattern emerged only among consumers with low self-brand connection, on social experience, satisfaction, perceived congruence, and customer experience, operating through perceived congruence. Therefore, Brand-AI congruency is conditional, holding for consumers without an established brand relationship.

items.title: Navigating Safety on BART: Understanding Rider Perceptions, Behaviors, and Design Opportunities
items.abstract: BART (Bay Area Rapid Transit) serves commuters, students, and visitors in the Bay Area. However, ridership has declined due to rising crimes, drug use, sexual assaults, and homelessness. These challenges disproportionately impact women and minorities, many of whom report discomfort, distrust in the system, and negative safety perceptions (Alliance for Girls Youth, 2024). The goal is to examine how safety perception influences BART riders’ experiences and decision making through the lenses of Human Factors and Industrial Engineering. We conducted a mixed-method research to understand perceived risk, environmental awareness, and support riders’ needs when commuting. Participants, particularly women, had reported feeling unsafe at night, traveling in groups, strategically choosing seatings, and staying vigilant in fear of being harmed. Riders also expressed interest in a verified “buddy feature,” safety alerts, and reporting incidents. Overall, this highlights opportunities to improve safety, build trust, and improve the commuting experience for BART.

items.title: Navigating Wicked Problems in Project Contexts: Adaptive Leadership as a Theoretical Lens for Understanding Project Managers’ Practices
items.abstract: This study examined how project managers navigate wicked problem dynamics in project environments with ambiguous problem definitions, contested stakeholder interests, evolving constraints, and no definitive solutions. Drawing on eight nested discussion sessions comprising 24 small-group conversations with 168 experienced project professionals across diverse industries, supplemented by 12 follow-up interviews, the study used a theory-informed abductive qualitative design. Adaptive leadership and wicked problem concepts informed the discussion prompts, whereas initial coding remained open to participants’ accounts rather than applying a predetermined adaptive-leadership coding framework. We then iteratively interpreted emergent patterns using wicked problems theory, adaptive leadership, and sensemaking as sensitizing theoretical lenses. The analysis identified five recurring adaptive practices: diagnostic framing, collaborative sensemaking, situational awareness, emotional regulation, and transparent communication. These practices illuminate how project managers develop workable problem definitions, engage competing perspectives, and coordinate action when technical expertise and established plans are insufficient. The study provides an empirically grounded account of leadership practice in temporary organizations and identifies practice-oriented implications for responding to wicked problem dynamics within time-bounded project settings.

items.title: Near-Real-Time Wildfire Segmentation and Brightness Temperature Estimation from Geostationary Satellite Imagery Using Deep Learning
items.abstract: Near-real-time wildfire monitoring is essential for situational awareness and emergency response. The Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) observes at 2 km every 5 min, whereas the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observes at 375 m twice daily, leaving neither sensor able to track rapidly evolving fires in fine spatial detail. This study introduces a two-step deep learning approach that statistically infers VIIRS-like sub-pixel fire segmentation and brightness temperature (BT) from GOES imagery. The dataset comprises 257 U.S. wildfires within preselected regions of interest, pairing multi-spectral GOES imagery with VIIRS-derived references in four classes (Non-Fire, Small, Medium, and Large) defined by the number of fire pixels. Against an autoencoder-based baseline, the proposed method raises average precision from 0.105 to 0.368 and reduces the fire region BT root mean square error by 72.1% from 81.33 K to 22.69 K. Omission error rates fall from 9.41% to 1.96% for Medium fires and remain at zero for Large fires, whereas Small fires, 37% of the test set, remain at 39.91%. The false positive rate on Non-Fire images falls from 66.86% to 8.48%, near the operational GOES product’s 6.36% with lower omission (31.40% versus 40.35%). Inference completes within 5 min of observation for a monitored region.

items.title: Norm Change and Renegotiation in Higher Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Conceptual Review from the Perspective of Social Network Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has disrupted the invisible normative infrastructure of universities at multiple points simultaneously. Unlike previous technological transitions, AI enters the higher education system concurrently through three interconnected levels: the student level, where the meaning of assignments, exams, and individual work is renegotiated; the faculty level, where authorship, peer review, course preparation, and assessment practices are reshaped; and the institutional level, where academic integrity policies, accreditation processes, and relations of trust with publishers are restructured. This simultaneous and systemic disruption produces a relational normative phenomenon that individualistic accounts of AI usage fail to adequately capture. This chapter develops a conceptual framework by bringing together social norm theory in the tradition of Bicchieri and Coleman, the structural social network analysis of Granovetter, Burt, Valente, and Centola, and the sociology of higher education following Bourdieu and Bernstein. It identifies five sets of norms undergoing simultaneous transformation (authorship and ownership of work, assessment and its meaning, pedagogical authority, knowledge ownership, and academic productivity expectations) and analyzes how four properties of academic networks (density, brokerage, centrality, and boundary permeability) shape the speed, direction, and stability of normative change. The primary contribution is a systemic reading that traces AI-induced norm flows vertically across student, faculty, and institutional levels. Here, AI is read not as a novel tool but as a relational actor circulating within academic networks, accelerating certain norms, eroding others, and triggering the emergence of new normative consensuses.

items.title: Opening ecological data to reduce bias and strengthen AI in ecology
items.abstract: In 1985, Richard Stallman introduced copyleft, a licensing principle that allows source code to be used, modified, and redistributed provided that the same freedoms are preserved in derivative works (Stallman, 1985). Although developed for software, copyleft offers a useful analogy for ecological research, where data, metadata, and analytical code should be accessible and reusable under clear licenses. Similarly, our ability to understand and address ecological challenges such as biodiversity loss, species range shifts, land degradation, and climate change depends on ecological knowledge being open where ethically appropriate and otherwise responsibly accessible. Such knowledge should also be managed according to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and established domain standards such as Darwin Core and Ecological Metadata Language (Wieczorek et al. 2012, Wilkinson et al. 2016). Despite substantial progress in open science (Dwivedi et al. 2022), many key ecological datasets (e.g., national ecological inventories, biodiversity records, and high-spatial- and temporal-resolution remote-sensing data) remain proprietary or available only with restricted access (e.g., requiring formal approval). These gaps are substantial: Large-scale analyses of hundreds of millions of ecological records reveal persistent taxonomic, geographic, and temporal biases (Meyer et al. 2015, Daru and Rodriguez, 2023). Much of the scientific literature also remains behind paywalls, while open-access publication fees can create barriers for researchers with limited funding (Rocchini and Neteler 2012). This paradox, that is, publicly funded knowledge becoming inaccessible to the public, constrains who can participate in ecological research and which ecosystems, regions, and perspectives are ultimately represented. AI does not create this problem but can amplify it by embedding data biases in models reused at scale, while closed training data limit independent scrutiny (Koch et al. 2022). AI for ecology encompasses task-specific machine-learning and computer-vision models, as well as foundation models, including large language models (LLMs). These systems differ in scale, purpose, and accessibility, but all depend on the quality, documentation, and governance of the data used to train and evaluate them. By integrating diverse data sources, AI can transform ecological research. However, when data, code, or model-development processes cannot be independently inspected, existing knowledge gaps and biases may be transferred into ecological inference. Appropriately open, reliable, and interoperable ecological data, together with transparent and auditable AI infrastructures, are therefore essential for robust, equitable, and epistemically sound ecological research. The expansion of AI in ecological research intensifies the need for transparent and well-documented knowledge. Bias is not unique to AI: statistical, mechanistic, and machine-learning models can all inherit limitations from their data and assumptions. AI can increase the scale, opacity, and reach of these effects (Han et al. 2023). Currently, many applications in ecology use task-specific AI models trained for bounded prediction or classification problems (Pichler and Hartig 2023). These models are often trained on specialized aggregated ecological repositories (e.g., biodiversity data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility [GBIF]), climatic variables (e.g., from WorldClim and ERA5), or land-use and land cover change mapping (e.g., from satellite imagery). In contrast, the rise of foundation models, including LLMs used for the automated synthesis of scientific literature, code generation, data processing and analysis, requires massive cross-domain training sets that are difficult to build from scratch. Consequently, models trained on skewed, geographically biased, or inaccessible datasets can systematically misrepresent under-sampled regions and reflect long-standing inequities in ecological knowledge. When training datasets are inaccessible, their composition is also difficult to inspect, making gaps in the representation of regions, languages, taxa, or perspectives harder to detect and evaluate. Thus, LLMs are not necessarily more biased than task-specific AI models, but their biases can be harder to trace and hence propagate across a wider range of users, tasks, and applications. In ecology, both task-specific and generic models inherit the limitations of the data used to train them. For example, species-recognition models inherit taxonomic imbalances in training images (Koch et al. 2022), whereas LLMs can process ecological information rapidly but may perform poorly on specific tasks. Gougherty and Clipp (2024) found that LLMs often struggled to extract pathogen-incidence values and sometimes inferred that all individuals were affected when no incidence value was reported. Similarly, Dorm et al. (2026) showed that LLMs performed poorly in generating species range maps and offered only limited improvement over random guessing in threat classification. Comparable effects have been observed in other AI domains, where imbalances in training data have produced systematically poorer model performance for underrepresented groups (Birhane, 2022). Together, these examples illustrate how unbalanced training data can transfer existing knowledge gaps into model outputs, highlighting the importance of identifying, documenting, and reducing such biases before models are applied beyond their validated domain. AI models can furthermore introduce subtler epistemic risks (Loru et al. 2025), including the confident fabrication of ecological information, the misrepresentation of species-trait responses to environmental gradients, and the generation of unsupported ecological interactions or spatial patterns. In ecological applications, documented limitations already include errors in quantitative information extraction and uneven performance across tasks (Gougherty and Clipp, 2024, Dorm et al. 2026). For these reasons, responsible openness and transparent governance of ecological data and metadata are vital, because the reliability of specialized models and large-scale synthesis depends on whether foundational ecological resources can be appropriately accessed, documented, and independently evaluated. Reproducible evaluation therefore requires practical commitments. Ecological AI studies should provide standardized documentation describing where their training data came from, which taxa, regions, and environmental conditions they cover, how the model is intended to be used, and its known limitations. Established tools such as datasheets for datasets and model cards can support this documentation (Gebru et al. 2021). Models should also be evaluated across taxa, regions, languages, and environmental conditions, and data, code, prompts, model weights, and independent evaluation sets should be released where ethically, legally, and technically possible (Maasri et al. 2022, Smith et al. 2024). In order to improve data exchange and utilization, general principles and standards for the creation, verification, and sharing of data should be established while respecting the owners and creators of specific databases. Any restrictions and access procedures should also be documented. Public initiatives such as the Minerva LLM (Orlando et al. 2024) illustrate the value of transparent, language-specific model development, but openness alone does not ensure ecological or cultural validity across regions. AI also changes the politics of openness by creating a risk that openly shared data and open-source code are incorporated into proprietary models without reciprocal access, attribution, credit, or participation for the researchers, developers, and communities who produced them. In public and public/private programs such as GenAI4EU (2025), adequate funding should mean sustained support for data curation, digitization of legacy records, targeted collection in documented gaps, local skills and infrastructure, and independent auditing, not only model development. Funders, publishers, scientific societies, and research institutions should recognize data curation as a research output and require transparent documentation and evaluation. Collaboration should connect local communities and data holders to national infrastructures, international repositories, and standards bodies. Identifying and reducing bias in AI development, enabling robust validation, and sustaining open infrastructures all depend fundamentally on the availability of high-quality, representative, and well-documented ecological data. Where data are scarce, uneven, or unreliable, transparency becomes especially important for identifying gaps and assessing their consequences (Titley et al. 2017). Open data and governance policies must therefore be accompanied by dedicated funding for targeted data collection, the digitization of legacy records, curation, metadata preparation, quality control, local computational infrastructure, training, and equitable collaboration, particularly in under-sampled regions. Such investments are necessary to prevent openness from disproportionately benefiting institutions that already possess the resources needed to exploit shared datasets. Openness should not, however, imply unrestricted public release. Precise locations of threatened species, Indigenous and local knowledge, and data governed by consent or legal agreements may require spatial generalization, controlled access, embargoes, or community authority (Tulloch et al. 2018). Data should instead be as open as possible and as protected as necessary, combining FAIR data stewardship with the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) where Indigenous or community-governed data are involved. International coordination among funders, ecological societies, repositories, publishers, data providers, and model developers is also needed to establish interoperable standards for data collection, annotation, documentation, sharing, and controlled access. Differences in the quality, resolution, and accessibility of ecological datasets should be explicitly documented and considered during model development and evaluation rather than remaining hidden (Dwivedi et al. 2022). Without shared standards and a commitment to responsible openness, ecological AI risks becoming fragmented, opaque, and shaped primarily by actors with the greatest computational and data resources. The practical priorities that we highlight are the following. Ecologists, AI researchers, funders, journals, repositories, and ecological societies should: audit geographic, taxonomic, temporal, and, where relevant, linguistic gaps in AI training and evaluation data, and quantify their effects on model performance; fund targeted data collection and the digitization of legacy records where these gaps have meaningful consequences; require machine-readable metadata and licenses, provenance records, uncertainty documentation, datasheets for datasets, and model cards; maintain independent benchmark datasets stratified across regions, taxa, sensors, and environmental conditions; and ensure that data-producing communities have access to computational infrastructure, training, credit, and decision-making roles rather than being treated solely as data providers (Wilkinson et al. 2016, Smith et al. 2024). Ecological research stands at a decisive crossroad: As AI reshapes how we observe and interpret the natural world, the openness and responsible governance of our data, models, and publications will determine whether this transformation is equitable and scientifically robust. Unrepresentative datasets, or data and models that cannot be independently evaluated, risk narrowing ecological insight, reinforcing global disparities, and introducing epistemic distortions that degrade our collective understanding of ecological systems. A well-governed, participatory, and inclusive ecological knowledge system, open where possible and protected where necessary, supported by public LLM research, auditable domain-specific models, and genuinely accessible publishing practices, is crucial to ensure that AI becomes a tool for discovery and justice rather than distortion. Just as copyleft preserved the freedoms to use, modify, and share software, responsible openness can free environmental science from informational silos while respecting legitimate restrictions. In the age of AI, openness is not only a technical requirement but an ethical obligation: Shared and responsibly governed knowledge is the foundation of collective solutions. items.title: Operationalizing biological interpretability in health-related visual stimuli using multimodal artificial intelligence as standardized non-human raters
items.abstract: Abstract Evaluation and assessment research in health communication requires structured, construct-based approaches for interpreting visual materials. This study introduces the Asclepius Biological Interpretability Scale, developed through a two-stage modified Delphi process (a joint image-and-item panel followed by an independent item-only panel) grounded in the Biopsychosocial Model and Visual Literacy Theory, and examines whether multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems can reproducibly apply this framework relative to internally generated human reference scores. Six artworks (four health-themed and two controls) were evaluated by three multimodal AI models and four researchers (internal human reference) using a standardized protocol with independent researcher-operated accounts, memory-isolation procedures, repeated assessments over two days, and the final 20-item scale. Because Image Type varied across only six stimuli, health-themed versus control differences were summarized at the image level (Cohen’s d), human–AI differences were summarized descriptively at the rater level, and reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Spearman correlations. Within this development image set, AI-generated scores were descriptively higher for health-themed than for control images on the three biomedical subscales (image-level Cohen’s d = 0.91–1.38) but not on Non-Medical Interpretability (d = 0.49); with four health-themed and two control images, these differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.19–0.60). Reproducibility across researcher-operated accounts was excellent for the three biomedical subscales (ICC = 0.90–0.97) and moderate for Non-Medical Interpretability (ICC = 0.57), whereas agreement across assessment days was poor (ICC = 0.04–0.46). The four researchers’ internal reference scores were higher than the AI-generated scores on the biomedical subscales for health-themed images (mean differences 1.41–1.96 points) and lower on Non-Medical Interpretability (− 2.02 to − 2.19 points). These findings provide preliminary methodological evidence that multimodal AI can reproducibly apply a structured interpretability framework to controlled visual stimuli. Although day-to-day stability and the Non-Medical Interpretability subscale, which showed substantial internal-consistency problems, require further refinement, the results support the feasibility of using AI as standardized non-human raters within controlled methodological settings. Broader validation using authentic health communication materials and independent external human raters remains necessary.

items.title: Optimizing ergonomics and productivity in automotive assembly lines: a bi-objective integer linear programming approach
items.abstract: Abstract The automotive industry’s operations face a critical dilemma: achieving high productivity while maintaining adequate ergonomic standards. High-volume production amplifies this condition, because the frequency of task execution keeps ergonomic risk ever-present. This work presents a real case from an automotive body parts assembly line. The objectives are to minimize the maximum individual ergonomic risk throughout job-rotation periods along a daily journey, and to optimize productivity by determining the optimal worker-to-workstation assignments. The Occupational Repetitive Action (OCRA) index is used to assess the risk of upper extremity musculoskeletal disorders. To solve this bi-objective problem, two algorithms are proposed: an $$\varepsilon $$ ε -constraint approach and a Tchebychev method. Both are grounded in a novel Integer Linear Programming (ILP) model tailored to integrate ergonomic and productivity considerations. The algorithms generated a complete Pareto front of 16 efficient solutions within a reasonable computational time. Managerial insights are derived, highlighting the inherent trade-off between the makespan and ergonomic risk, providing valuable guidelines for balancing worker well-being and productivity in assembly-line operations.

items.title: Organizational Readiness In Artificial Intelligence Implementation: The Role of Digital Transformation In Bank Indonesia
items.abstract: This study analyzes the relationship between digitalization, structural transformation, and carbon emission intensity in six ASEAN countries, namely Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Cambodia. The study uses annual panel data for the period 2004–2024, with the main estimation period covering 2010–2024. Carbon emission intensity is used as the dependent variable, while the number of internet users, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, international trade, and services sector value added are used as independent variables. All variables are transformed into natural logarithms so that the coefficients can be interpreted as elasticities. Estimation is conducted using the Fixed Effects Model with period fixed effects and Panel EGLS with period weights following model selection tests. The results show that digitalization, proxied by the number of internet users, has a positive but statistically insignificant relationship with carbon emission intensity. In contrast, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, and international trade have positive and significant relationships. Services sector value added has a negative and significant relationship with carbon emission intensity. These findings indicate that structural transformation toward the services sector is associated with lower emission intensity, while industrial expansion, urbanization, economic growth, and trade are associated with increased carbon emission intensity in the countries examined.

items.title: PAI Students’ Perceptions of Ethics in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Learning
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.

items.abstract: This article examines the linguodidactic foundations for forming and developing the AI competence of both educators and students within the context of the effective use of artificial intelligence technologies in language education. Amidst digital transformation, artificial intelligence-specifically generative language models, chatbots, speech recognition systems, automated assessment tools, and adaptive learning platforms-is becoming a new component of the foreign language teaching and learning process. The article defines an educator's AI competence as a composite of technological knowledge, methodological-pedagogical competence, critical evaluation skills, awareness of ethics and digital security, and the ability to integrate AI tools into language education.

items.title: Pemberdayaan Pokdarwis Melalui Layanan Suara Berbasis AI di Desa Wisata Kelawi
items.abstract: Kelawi Tourism Village, South Lampung, has strong community-based tourism potential, but the Minang Rua Bahari Tourism Awareness Group (Pokdarwis) faces communication barriers when serving international visitors. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to strengthen Pokdarwis capacity through an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted voice service as a communication support tool. The program was conducted from 12 to 14 June 2026 and involved 15 Pokdarwis members. Activities included problem identification, local knowledge development and validation, QR-based service implementation, training, mentoring, and evaluation at four service points: visitor reception, turtle conservation, Green Canyon, and homestay and culinary services. Results showed an increase in partner capacity from 58.2% in the pre-test to 91.8% in the post-test, representing a 33.6 percentage-point improvement. Participant satisfaction reached 92%, while partner and visitor achievement rates reached 95.2% and 94.5%, respectively. The program demonstrates that AI can support communication, conservation, safety, and the delivery of local cultural and culinary information without replacing the role of Pokdarwis.

items.title: Pengembangan Video Edukasi K3 untuk Pembelajaran Praktikum Teknik Jaringan Tenaga Listrik (Development of Occupational Safety and Health Educational Videos for Electric Power Network Technology Practicum Learning)
items.abstract: Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) is an essential component of practical learning in the Electric Power Network Engineering (TJTL) program because students are exposed to electrical and workshop hazards. This study aimed to develop an OHS educational video and determine its feasibility, student response, and the increase in students’ understanding after use. The study employed Research and Development (R&D) with the 4-D model consisting of Define, Design, Develop, and Disseminate. Product validation involved three expert validators consisting of one media expert and two OHS experts, while user feasibility was assessed by three teacher practitioners. Student response involved 29 students, and the increase in understanding was examined using a one-group pretest-posttest design and N-Gain analysis. The mean feasibility score was 4.50 from the expert-media assessment and 4.82 from the practitioner assessment, both in the “very good” category. Student response reached a mean score of 4.78, also in the “very good” category. The mean N-Gain was 0.86, classified as high, indicating a substantial increase in test scores after the video was used. The findings support the use of the video as a contextual learning aid for OHS preparation before TJTL practical activities. However, the effectiveness evidence is limited because the study used one group without a comparison group and measured cognitive understanding rather than actual safety behavior.
